articles.content_orig:

Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with cancer and has had the lower lobe of his right lung removed during surgery on Tuesday , according to the Vatican.
Tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer, the Vatican said. The diagnosis had been suspected during preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.
The 71-year-old pontiff spent around three hours in the operating room, and the surgery itself took around 90 minutes.
“In order to make the procedure curative, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique,” wrote lead surgeon Professor Stefano Margaritora.
"A rapid intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as had been suspected from the pre-operative tests.”
The Vatican said the surgery was successful and there were no complications. Afterwards, Pope Leo was awake and resting in his hospital room .
Dozens of well-wishers greeted him at the hospital before the procedure.
In a rare level of transparency, the Pope revealed the discovery of a small nodule on his lung during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3cm (1.2ins) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. The scans are often done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening.
A nodule may be benign or malignant, and surgical removal is often recommended to establish whether it is cancer, and to treat a malignancy while it is still localised.
Before the procedure, oncologists said that even if the growth proved to be cancerous, Leo’s prognosis was “excellent” because it would be removed at an early stage.
The Vatican has cancelled all of Leo’s audiences for a week while he recovers.
The Pope is known to be sporty and in good shape, playing tennis weekly and swimming. The lung surgery is believed to be his second spell in hospital.
He came down with typhoid fever as a young missionary priest in 1985, soon after arriving in Chulucanas, Peru. The illness and hospital stay were a cathartic moment for him to decide to stay in the poverty and discomfort of Peru after living in relative comfort in Rome — a decision that ultimately paved the way to his papacy, according to an interview he gave to Elise Ann Allen last year for Pope Leo XIV: The Biography .
According to the book, Leo said he prayed to God to let him die rather than suffer the “horrible” pain of the fever. “I was hooked up to an IV, and I said, ‘If this is your sense of humour, Lord, I think you could do a little better’.
“Obviously, I survived; I recovered, but it turned out to be a very significant moment for me, because it was like, ‘Well, you’ve already dealt with the illness; you already see what the needs are here — the order, the Augustinians, the church are telling you, ‘We need you here; go for it.’ I never looked back.”

articles.title_orig: Cornell suspends fraternity parties amid backlash over alleged sexual assault
articles.title_zh: Cornell suspends fraternity parties amid backlash over alleged sexual assault
articles.content_orig:
State officials and others have criticised how Cornell and local prosecutors handled the case
Cornell University is banning all parties at fraternity houses as the school faces  backlash over its handling of an alleged sexual assault on campus two years ago.
Last month, a woman known as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit alleging she was plied with drugs and raped by several men in 2024 at a party at a Cornell fraternity house.
In a statement on Tuesday, Cornell's president, Michael Kotlikoff, announced a series of measures responding to the alleged assault, including the end to fraternity parties for the rest of the school year.
"I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community," he said.
Cornell students voice frustration at public hearing over rape case
"It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," he added.
Fraternities have existed at university campuses across the US for decades and function as all-male social clubs where the students live, study and socialise. Over the years, the groups have become notorious for binge-drinking, partying and dangerous hazing rituals.
In a statement, a lawyer representing Doe said she filed a civil lawsuit "to achieve her aim of improving Cornell and its response to abuse claims".
"While the steps announced today are helpful to achieve this goal, they are too late to protect Ms. Doe," said lawyer Thomas Giuffra.
Cornell's president said anyone who violated the new fraternity party policy at the New York university would be suspended.
The school also said it planned to improve support for survivors of sexual assault, including more staff to help people report sexual misconduct and navigate other support systems as well.
Through Title IX, the federal law that governs how universities handle sexual assault claims, schools are required to provide measures of support to help survivors stay in school after assaults. Doe's lawyer has said she dropped out after the alleged assault.
Cornell case highlights 'draining' maze for victims to report campus sex assaults
The president said the school will allow New York State Police's trauma-informed officers to investigate allegations of sexual assault on its campus.
These officers will interview survivors who want to pursue criminal charges and prepare "comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency", Kotlikoff said.
Cornell has faced criticism over the information shared with the local district attorney's office about Jane Doe's allegations.
Out of hundreds of documents that US media outlets have obtained from Cornell's investigation into the assault, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said that in 2024, his office received only a six-page statement signed by the victim as well as Snapchat messages in which the men at the fraternity party advertised a free sexual encounter with Doe.
State officials have also criticised Van Houten's decision not to bring charges or interview victims and witnesses himself. New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, to investigate the case.
Kotlikoff said Cornell would be bringing in national sexual violence prevention experts to examine "the factors leading to campus sexual violence and strategies to promote responsible sexual citizenship".
He said the steps were the first toward "systematic change" on campus.

articles.title_orig: China's export engine hits fastest pace since February with 36% growth
articles.title_zh: China's export engine hits fastest pace since February with 36% growth
articles.content_orig:
China's producer price index climbed at its fastest pace in over four years, rising 5% in September as higher fuel prices pushed up costs for businesses.
The increase was higher than the 4.5% expected by economists polled by Reuters, and sharply up from  the 3.8% seen in the previous month.
China's National Bureau of Statistics said higher prices were also seen in the country's coal sector, due to increased demand for coal for winter heating, temporary tight supply in major coal-producing areas, and expectations of rising international coal prices.
Consumer prices saw a 0.9% rise, marginally missing expectations of 1%, but up from 0.8% in the month before.
The increase in the consumer inflation rate was due to gasoline prices, which climbed 16.6% and contributed approximately 0.47 percentage points to the year-on-year CPI increase, according to Dong Lijuan, chief statistician of the Urban Division at the NBS.
This was partially offset by a wider fall in food prices, which declined 1.7% and pulled down the CPI by 0.29 percentage points, Dong added.
The core CPI rate, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, climbed 1%.
The lower-than-expected CPI reading indicates that domestic demand remains "lackluster," according to Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, in a note after the data release.
However, the higher PPI is pointing to an economy that is gradually moving away from deflationary pressures even if the recovery remains uneven, said Hao Zhou, chief economist at Guotai Junan International Holdings.
His view was that domestic demand was recovering more gradually than the industrial sector, although the fact that consumer inflation has remained in positive territory indicated at the deflationary environment in 2024 and 2025 "is continuing to fade."
The higher inflation figures come as China's economy grapples with its lowest growth rate in more than three years . GDP growth for the second quarter of the year missed expectations at 4.3%.
While economic data for August showed that retail sales expanded more slowly than expected, industrial output beat expectations.
On Sept 28, a State Council readout signaled that more policy support could be on the way for the Chinese economy, saying that "In response to emerging challenges in the economy's operation, efforts should be made to intensify counter-cyclical adjustment of macro policies."
Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING, wrote that "It marks a bit of a shift in tone," adding that more policy support rollouts will be coming so as to reach both short- and long-term growth targets.
"These include the 4.5%-5.0% GDP growth target for 2026, and the longstanding goal to double GDP from 2020 to 2035."

articles.title_orig: Launch of 13 new African National Youth Chapters of the World Food Forum
articles.title_zh: Launch of 13 new African National Youth Chapters of the World Food Forum
articles.content_orig:
Thirteen new World Food Forum (WFF) National Youth Chapters in Africa have joined the growing network of young leaders working to transform agrifood systems across the continent. They are in: Benin, Botswana, Burundi, Comoros, Democratic Republic of Congo, Eswatini, Gabon, Lesotho, Namibia, Nigeria, São Tomé and Príncipe, Senegal and Togo.
These new chapters bring the total number of National Youth Chapters in Africa to 33.
Speaking at the launch during the Global Youth Forum of the World Food Forum, FAO Assistant Director-General and Regional Representative for Africa Abebe Haile-Gabriel emphasized the importance of sustained investment in youth leadership.
“The real measure of success will be our ability to sustain this momentum, scale investment, and ensure that young people are not just beneficiaries of change, but architects of Africa's agrifood systems transformation,” he said.
Creating opportunities for youth leadership
The National Youth Chapters provide platforms for young people to connect, share knowledge, build partnerships and contribute to agrifood systems transformation at national and regional levels.
With more than 60 percent of Africa's population under the age of 25, expanding opportunities for young people to participate in decision-making, innovation and entrepreneurship is critical to the continent's future.
FAO is strengthening youth engagement across Africa through capacity-building initiatives, partnerships and opportunities for young agripreneurs to contribute to policy discussions.
Young agribusiness entrepreneurs and advocates from across Africa are participating at the World Food Forum in Rome this week. Youth leadership will also feature prominently at the upcoming Africa Science & Innovation Forum taking place in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, from 27 to 29 October.
Empowering Africa’s youth was also the focus of a session at the World Food Forum today titled Leading from the Front: Africa’s Youth Driving Agrifood Systems Transformation, featuring FAO’s Abebe Haile-Gabriel and Lesotho’s Minister of Agriculture, Food Security and Nutrition, Selibe Mochoboroane. The session focused on expanding opportunities for young Africans to lead innovation, entrepreneurship and job creation across agrifood systems. Haile-Gabriel emphasized the importance of investing in young people's skills, improving access to finance and technology, and ensuring young people have a meaningful role in shaping policies and investments.
The 13 new chapters join existing chapters in Cabo Verde, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia, the Gambia, Ghana, Kenya, Liberia, Madagascar, Malawi, Mauritius, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, Somalia, South Africa, South Sudan, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

Talarico has said he was sick with the flu, dispelling rumors that circulated among right-wing circles that he had been treated for mental health reasons at an Ohio clinic.

In the third Maine Senate debate, Republican Sen. Susan Collins presented herself as a uniquely capable senator using her seniority as chair of the Appropriations Committee to deliver for Maine.
She highlighted her push to extract federal funds early under the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program to assist with rising energy costs.
"I was successful just recently at getting the earliest release of the LIHEAP money ever, a month earlier than we mandated by law. Because we know people are filling up their oil tanks right now, and they need help," she said.
Collins took credit for the Defense Department's agreeing to support a second guided-missile destroyer expected to be built at Bath Iron Works facilities, which remains subject to congressional approval in an upcoming funding bill.

âDonât act like I donât know what Iâm talking about, because I do,â he said.
In her closing statement, Collins noted that the Constitution guarantees every state two senators. "It does not guarantee that all 100 senators will have the same knowledge, experience and clout," she said. "So when you live in a small state like Maine, who you send to Washington really matters."
Trump pardoned two people onstage during his rally in Wasilla, Alaska.
Zachary Czuback and Patrick Fleming, who co-owned a vehicle repair shop in Anchorage, pleaded guilty in 2022 to violating the Clean Air Act by tampering with devices that were federally mandated and monitored vehiclesâ diesel emissions.
Czuback was sentenced to five years of probation, a $66,000 fine and 180 hours of community service. Fleming was sentenced to pay a $66,000 fine.
âWe take protecting the environment seriously in Alaska and we wonât hesitate to prosecute individuals committing environmental crimes,â U.S. Attorney S. Lane Tucker for the District of Alaska said in a news release about the guilty plea.
Trump said onstage: âThey want to put them in jail for 10 years because they fixed an engine. How sick! Now, if you murder somebody, no problem, unless a Republican does the murdering. Then itâs the electric chair, right?â

The two then gave brief remarks. Czuback thanked Trump for the pardon, while Fleming boosted his endorsed candidates.
âIâll cut to the chase here, and letâs re-elect Dan Sullivan. Letâs re-elect Nick [Begich]. Letâs get it, Don. Thank you,â Fleming said.
Trump criticized ranked choice voting tonight in Alaska, telling supporters they should vote to repeal it on a ballot measure in the midterm elections.
He told them to "make sure you vote yes on the ballot measure to repeal" the 2020 ballot measure that enacted ranked choice voting in Alaska elections. The proposed ballot measure would also get rid of open primaries in the state, instead splitting primaries into those closed to one political party.
On ranked choice voting, Trump said: "It's a scam. It's a Democrat scam, and you got to repeal it."
Trump kicked off his rally in Alaska by urging the audience to vote for the "real Dan Sullivan" in the midterm election.
"On Nov. 3rd, we're going to send one of the best and most respected senators in D.C., Dan Sullivan, the real Dan Sullivan," Trump said, referring to Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.
Trump called Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher who is also running as a Republican for the Senate seat , "the fake Dan Sullivan" who was "put up by the Democrats."
"No, we can't let that happen. It's just cheating. Terrible," Trump said. "They put him up to get a little confused."
"So you gotta remember Dan Sullivan, Republican incumbent," he added.
Trump today questioned why Black voters would back Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, adding a new attack against the Democrat after having ripped into him at a rally yesterday in Ohio.
"Why would black people vote for Mohammed El-Sayed," wrote on Truth Social , claiming without evidence that El-Sayed has openly disparaged Black voters. He also referred to El-Sayed, who is Muslim, by his middle name, Mohamed.
In the Democratic primary, Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., outperformed El-Sayed in counties that have higher Black populations . Black voters have been a crucial bloc for Democrats in Michigan elections.
Trump's post came the same day that El-Sayed's opponent, Republican Mike Rogers, posted an ad featuring Black Democratic voters who said they would not be supporting El-Sayed.

Attorneys with the Trump-aligned group, writing on behalf of a number of Trump-affiliated lawyers, say Eastman's disbarment proceeding was part of âa concerted, nationwide effort by former government officials and advocacy groups to coopt state bar proceedings to punish, threaten, and drive attorneys out of the legal profession simply because they represented President Trump.â

articles.title_orig: Bank of America Fined $1.2 Billion for Lax Money-Laundering Oversight
articles.title_zh: Bank of America Fined $1.2 Billion for Lax Money-Laundering Oversight
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Regulators fined Bank of America ( BAC ) more than $1.2 billion on Tuesday over widespread failures in the banking giant's safeguards against money laundering and other illicit financial activity.
The Treasury Department said the nation's second-largest bank failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions and to report more than $5 billion in suspicious activity, including transactions potentially tied to Chinese money-laundering networks, narcotics trafficking, and fraud.
The enforcement actions include a $1.2 billion penalty from the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the third-largest fine in the Treasury Department's history after it fined crypto exchange Binance $3.4 billion in 2023 and TD Bank for $1.3 billion in 2024. The fine also includes a $750 million penalty from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), the largest ever imposed by that regulator.
The OCC penalty will be credited against FinCEN's assessment rather than added to it. Separately, a $11.6 million sanctions settlement brings the total penalties to more than $1.21 billion.
"Even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.
Bank of America's stock fell more than 2% after markets closed on Tuesday. It reports third quarter earnings Wednesday morning.
The bank said it will include a "non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share" in its third quarter results.
"Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right," a Bank of America spokesperson said in an email statement, adding that the Charlotte, North Carolina based lender has invested "billions of dollars in technology" and dedicated "thousands of employees to combat financial crime" to resolve the deficiencies.
Regulators said Bank of America's failures extended across its transaction monitoring systems, customer due diligence, and internal oversight.
The bank failed to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, including over $1 billion involving national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks.
FinCEN said Bank of America admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act and had effectively outsourced substantial portions of its suspicious activity detection responsibilities to law enforcement and other financial institutions.
The bank also prioritized revenue over compliance resources, according to Treasury, allowing suspicious transactions to go uninvestigated for extended periods.
The penalties come nearly two years after Bank of America agreed to a December 2024 cease-and-desist order requiring it to address longstanding weaknesses in its anti-money laundering controls.
The OCC said the bank failed to make sufficient progress despite that earlier enforcement action.
"Bank of America's poor response to its [Bank Secrecy Act] deficiencies is unacceptable," Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould said, describing continued breakdowns in internal controls.
Separately, Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control announced an $11.6 million settlement involving 475 apparent violations of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Iran, and other countries and activities.
As part of the latest enforcement actions, Bank of America must conduct a review of previously undetected suspicious transactions with an outside party and undergo independent assessments of its compliance controls.
Mike Mayo, a Wells Fargo equity analyst who covers the bank called the action a "black eye" for Bank of America while describing the one-time charge as "digestible."

articles.title_orig: F.B.I. Arrests OpenAI Employee Accused of Planting Bug in Office
articles.title_zh: F.B.I. Arrests OpenAI Employee Accused of Planting Bug in Office
articles.content_orig:
Prosecutors released CCTV images of the suspect allegedly checking on the secret recorder
A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.
OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee.
Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.
OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired.
According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.
Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product.
Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say.
On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said.
OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier".
According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment.
Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege.
He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'".
The device was allegedly concealed in toilet paper
On 5 October, prosecutors say he allegedly returned to inspect the device in the office room. Prosecutors used CCTV camera footage to link him to the scene.
That same day, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different part of the building. A security team for OpenAI opened it to find his wallet and ID, as well as another recording device that was similar to the one found in the office conference room, prosecutors said.
Alfozan appeared in court on Tuesday. It's unclear whether he has legal representation.
If found guilty, he faces up to five years in prison and a fine of $250,000 (Â£187,000).

articles.title_orig: In heated Georgia Senate debate, Jon Ossoff says he won’t run for president in 2028
articles.title_zh: In heated Georgia Senate debate, Jon Ossoff says he won’t run for president in 2028
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., said Tuesday night during a debate that he will not run for president in 2028.
Ossoff made the statement in response to a question as he faced off with his Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins. Ossoff is seeking a second six-year term in Georgia and said he would serve the full term.
“I have zero interest in running for president,” Ossoff said when he was asked directly by one of the moderators. “I’m not running for president. I’m running for re-election to the Senate.”
Ossoff has been regularly discussed as a potential Democratic contender in 2028. If he were to win the presidency, he would have to give up his Senate seat, which he stressed Tuesday night that he would not do.
After the brief remark, Ossoff quickly transitioned to pressing Collins about why he has supported President Donald Trump’s tariffs, a main focus of both his campaign and a debate the two held last week . Tuesday was the second debate in the nationally watched Georgia Senate race, this one organized by the Atlanta Press Club.
Collins quipped that Ossoff was actually trying to run for president and will be “your DSA candidate,” a reference to the Democratic Socialists of America.
The exchange came at the beginning of the hourlong debate, which covered ground including data centers; the economy under Trump, whose approval rating is at record lows; the war in Iran; and the issue of Collins’ son-in-law’s promoting white nationalist posts on social media.
Ossoff asked Collins directly whether he considered himself a “white nationalist.”
“I condemn any sort of hate speech,” Collins said. “Antisemitism, hate of any kind. It’s abhorrent.”
The exchange continued when Collins again asked Ossoff to denounce Reid Hoffman, a major donor to Democratic causes — including Ossoff-aligned political committees — whose name appeared in the Epstein files . Collins brought up Hoffman several times last week and did so again during the second debate.
Ossoff did not directly respond, and he again pointed to the fact that those close to Collins amplified white nationalists’ posts.
“How weak a person do you have to be to be unable to stop someone under your own roof from disseminating neo-Nazi propaganda while you run for Senate?” Ossoff said. “The paper reported it’s still going on today.”
Given a chance to respond, Collins did not address it directly. But he said rhetoric like Ossoff’s had motivated a New York man who is accused of making death threats against him.
“I’m a little tired of this, Jon,” Collins said. “This crazy person is in jail right now because of your rhetoric.”
Neither candidate directly answered the other’s charges.
Collins also, once again, did not answer questions about whether or not Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election. He was asked about audio of a call Trump made after the 2020 election asking Georgia Republican Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to “ find 11,780 votes ” to help overturn the 2020 election.
“You know, Joe Biden went into office, and boy, Georgians paid for it,” Collins said.
Matt Dixon is a senior national politics reporter for NBC News, based in Florida.

It is the second time in two months that a Taiwanese drone supplier has been investigated by the island’s authorities over the alleged use of prohibited mainland components.
Prosecutors in the northern city of Taoyuan said on Monday that Jiin Ming Industry and its subsidiary were suspected of installing mainland-made chips and camera lenses in military drones.

articles.title_orig: What we know about the man who died falling from a Six Flags rollercoaster
articles.title_zh: What we know about the man who died falling from a Six Flags rollercoaster
articles.content_orig:
Warning: This story includes distressing content
A man has died after falling from a rollercoaster at a Six Flags amusement park on Monday in the US state of Georgia.
The man, Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, was found dead under the ride after being ejected and hitting other people on it, according to police.
An investigation is under way and few details have yet to be released about what happened. Six Flags, the largest amusement park operator in North America, has temporarily closed nine rides across the US and Canada as a precaution.
Here's what we know so far about the incident.
The Cobb County Police Department said the incident at the Six Flags Over Georgia park happened just before 16:00 local time (20:00 GMT) on Monday.
"Officers working at the park responded to an incident involving a male guest on a roller coaster," it said in a statement on Tuesday.
"Preliminary information gathered through witness and employee interview indicates Kariem was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction."
The ride involved has not been specified but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, and multiple witnesses have identified the ride as the one involved in the incident.
The office of the state's insurance and fire safety commissioner, which enforces amusement park safety rules in Georgia, is also conducting a review.
Officials have not held a news conference on the incident.
The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five.
The company said in a statement that it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident" and that "our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones".
Nick Mendenhall said he witnessed the fatal moments in disbelief, watching the man come out of his seat and then fall into another cart on the ride before falling to the ground.
"It was just super, super bizarre, traumatic. I mean, it took me a couple of seconds, I feel like, to process what was going on," he told the AP. "I cant believe that I just saw that."
He said his mind instantly went to the trauma of all of those impacted by what he witnessed, including the man's loved ones and everyone who was on the ride with him.
One witness told NBC affiliate WXIA that the incident was captured in souvenir photos that were automatically taken of the rollercoaster while it was in motion. The BBC has not been able to verify this statement.
Connor Thompson told the BBC's US partner CBS News that he was in line for the ride when everyone started "yelling, clearly distressed".
"Everyone was kind of confused at first, and then there was someone who was  yelling, 'Call 911! Someone fell out!" he said. "At first it was almost like I didn't believe it because I thought that was like impossible for something like that to happen."
He said he saw the cart come into the hub where others were waiting in line and could see the restraint was unlatched.
Another witness, CiCi Nelson, told CNN she, too, was in line to ride the Goliath when the rollercoaster returned and she saw an empty seat with a loose safety bar and a female covered in blood.
Nelson described a scene of hysteria, adding that one man was "freaking out, saying someone fell off".
Brittany Landry, who believed she saw Kariem ejected from the rollercoaster, told Fox News she was in tears.
"I broke because we were just on there," she said.
Kariem's family said he was a father, passionate educator and had survived two bouts of cancer.
His family told WXIA that he had survived cancer twice - the last stint in 2018 - and was in a car crash with his 10-year-old daughter three weeks before his death.
He lived in the nearby city of Atlanta and worked for Wesley International Academy, a public charter school, for more than 12 years as an IT manager, technology teacher and robotics coach.
"Mr. Kariem was deeply loved and respected, and his absence will be felt throughout our school community," the school said in a statement posted to its Facebook account.
"His love for Wesley, dedication to our students, and commitment to our school community were evident in everything he did."
Outside of work, Kariem enjoyed creating products with his laser engraver and 3D printers, as well as cooking, watching anime and spending time with family and friends, according to his profile on the school's website.
The death at Six Flags Over Georgia is at least the seventh there, according to the Doan Law Firm, which tracks amusement park accidents and represents victims.
According to the firm, this includes two people who had medical emergencies, two who were in restricted areas when they were struck by a ride, two who died in car-related accidents and one who died months after using the park's pool.
Six Flags operates 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico.
In the last 15 years, two deaths caused by falling from the park's rollercoasters led to lawsuits and settlements. One in 2011 involved an Iraq War veteran who was ejected from a ride in New York and hit his head on the car. In the other, in 2013, a woman slipped from her restraints on a rollercoaster in Texas and fell 75 feet.
In September, the Six Flags Magic Mountain park in California announced it was closing its X2 rollercoaster after more 100 people alleged that they had suffered brain injuries from the ride.
With additional reporting by Brandon Drenon

articles.title_orig: Saudi Energy Giant Struck as War Spikes Between Houthis and Saudi Arabia
articles.title_zh: Saudi Energy Giant Struck as War Spikes Between Houthis and Saudi Arabia
articles.content_orig:
Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis traded fresh strikes on energy infrastructure, with the Iran-backed group again targeting the Saudi capital and appearing to hit the headquarters of Saudi state oil giant Aramco.
An administrative building belonging to Aramco in the Eastern Province city of Dhahran, where the company is headquartered, was targeted, according to Saudi authorities. It caused a limited fire, but it’s not clear if this was due to a direct hit or to falling debris. No injuries were reported.
The Saudi-led coalition also said it had intercepted and destroyed three cruise missiles and two drones targeting the Riyadh region and southern Saudi Arabia. At least four people were injured from falling debris, according to Saudi authorities.
CNN has reached out to Aramco for comment.
It marked the latest escalation between the two sides, following a week of deadly Houthi missile and drone attacks that shut Riyadh’s main international airport .
The strikes also came just hours after Saudi Arabia attacked a key fuel depot on Tuesday, which it claims was being used by Houthi rebels to support strikes on the kingdom’s airports and energy facilities – as well as attacks on shipping in the Red Sea.
Earlier, the Houthi-controlled Yemen Oil Company had said that the facility held no stocks of petroleum products, and that an attack would not affect fuel reserves or supplies.
The strikes killed two civilians and injured two, according to the Houthis, though the Saudi-led coalition insisted it had warned civilians to leave the area beforehand.
“This operation focused on neutralizing the capabilities the Houthi militia uses to threaten the kingdom, Yemen, the southern Red Sea and maritime corridors,” coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said in a statement.
Tuesday’s exchange comes amid signs the long-running conflict, which reignited this summer and intensified last month after years of relative calm, is continuing to escalate.
Earlier Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile launched toward its eastern province, and another aimed at Haradh near the Yemeni border. It also reported intercepting three Houthi drones north of Riyadh.
Meanwhile, Houthi-run Al Masirah TV reported that artillery fire by the Saudi-led coalition in Saada province wounded three Yemenis and two African residents in Baqim district. It later reported that two civilians were killed and two others wounded by artillery fire on residential villages in the border district of Shada in Sadaa, and also reported strikes in Sanaa and several other provinces. CNN cannot independently verify the reports.
The conflict has been intensifying since the Houthis announced in July that — in response to what they say is retaliation for a Saudi blockade on the Yemeni capital — they would target Saudi shipping in the Red Sea as well as infrastructure inside the kingdom.
Those attacks have stepped up in recent days, including with repeated strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, where 13 people were killed and more than 300 wounded on Saturday in what was the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
Why billions spent on defense haven’t shielded Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
The US, UK, Spain and Canada are among countries now warning their citizens against using the airport. Meanwhile, the US State Department on Tuesday expanded travel restrictions for US government personnel in the kingdom, saying employees now require special authorization from the chief of mission to use any airport in Saudi Arabia.
The attacks have also exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom’s defense capabilities as it wages its air campaign in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which is fighting the Houthis on the ground.
On Tuesday, the Yemeni government forces claimed to have made continued advances in the military operation, dubbed “Dawn of Yemen.” It said that in the past 24 hours its forces had carried out 2,200 strikes against Houthi positions, killing about 1,200 fighters and destroying or disabling more than 440 military vehicles and other assets. CNN could not independently verify the figures.
Meanwhile, the Houthis vowed further attacks against economic and aviation targets within Saudi Arabia, warning that they would target facilities belonging to Aramco as well as the King Khalid International Airport if Saudi forces continued attacking them.
CNN’s Eyad Kourdi contributed to the report.

articles.title_orig: Graduate student accused of poisoning colleague and trying to flee to China arrested at LAX
articles.title_zh: Graduate student accused of poisoning colleague and trying to flee to China arrested at LAX
articles.content_orig:
Microbiologist Aili Wang, 32, poisoned tea of colleague in Wyoming who had pending patents, prosecutors allege
A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she did not get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her.
Aili Wang, 32, was arrested 6 October at Los Angeles international airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China . With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment – research similar to work she had done in China.
Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles. She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim’s wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.
US officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from American universities.
The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations left him reeling. He was uncertain if the victim will fully recover.
“It’s been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your students’ lives is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that,” Gomelsky told the Associated Press. “That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career.”
Wang had no attorney listed in court documents. The AP tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.
The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as “KT”, began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical in the coffee maker water. The victim and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie.
Wang allegedly was recorded 27 September going through the alleged victim’s desk. On 1 October, she was recorded “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer’s affidavit said.
Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit.
The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a prestigious conference in August, Gomelsky said.
He also noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said. When he washed the coffee maker, Gomelsky said, the taste would go away.
Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the graduate student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.
Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine.
It’s not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany county circuit court judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors’ request and raised bond to $1.5m cash-only.
Wang allegedly asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer, police said.

articles.title_orig: Texas DA says ICE intentionally hit immigrant with a car and may have withheld evidence
articles.title_zh: Texas DA says ICE intentionally hit immigrant with a car and may have withheld evidence
articles.content_orig:
HOUSTON — Videos collected by local investigators make it “pretty obvious” that an ICE officer intentionally ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez during an immigration stop Saturday, which could lead to assault charges, the district attorney said Tuesday.
“This was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told NBC News.
Teare said the federal government is not cooperating with the investigation conducted by his office and the Harris County Sheriff’s Office. He also said ICE may have allowed the erasure of critical data in the vehicle involved in striking Parra, who was on foot.
Teare said that in his seven years as a Harris County vehicular crimes division chief, he has reviewed video from a number of other auto-pedestrian collision cases. He said the video his investigators have gathered in Parra’s case “goes above” the video that was posted online and obtained by NBC affiliate KPRC of Houston.
“My viewing of it, and many other investigators that have viewed it, as well, it’s pretty obvious that this was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” he said.
Parra, 48, was left with multiple breaks and fractures in his body, according to his attorney and an advocate who has been speaking on his behalf. He had surgery on one leg and faces multiple additional operations, said Cesar Espinosa, co-founder and executive director of FIEL, an immigrant civil rights group.
Video obtained by KPRC shows a white truck headed in the opposite direction of traffic on a busy roadway. It shows a vehicle jumping a yellow median and heading in the direction that Parra is running.
It then appears to show the vehicle, which is not marked, swerving left toward Parra’s path, in front of a truck stopped in a shopping center. The parked truck leaves, and a man can be seen on the pavement behind the ICE vehicle, the video shows.
An ICE spokesman said over the weekend that officers were pursuing the fleeing men and that “Miguel Parra Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.”
Teare, a Democrat, announced late Monday that his office had launched an independent investigation.
On Tuesday, an ICE spokesperson who was not identified said in a statement that “allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE. The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct.”
ICE said the allegations are “disgusting smears” that are “peddled by the media,” leading to more than a 1,600% increase in assaults and a 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks against its law enforcement officers. It did not offer data behind those numbers.
ICE has said that Parra was not the target of the attempted stop but that he was in the country illegally. Parra’s attorney and family have said he has no criminal record and was on his way to work applying stucco.
Teare said his office and the sheriff’s office determined that the vehicle that struck Parra was a Jeep Cherokee and that it potentially had evidence, including a data crash recorder. He said his office wanted to know whether the vehicle locked in information at the time of the collision that could be downloaded, such as speed, steering and braking. Teare said the way to preserve data from the car would have been to “put it on a flatbed trailer and you take it to forensically download it.”
But he said he believes any data on the recorder related to the incident could have been erased when ICE drove the car away.
He and the sheriff’s investigators told ICE the information needed to be downloaded, but ICE refused, Teare said.
ICE did not respond to questions about a data crash recorder, the erasing of any potential data or any refusal to download it.
“Our office began drafting a search warrant that we were in the process of drafting when the ICE agent in question, the one that had been driving, we believed, at the time of the collision, jumped back into the car and drove it away from the scene,” Teare said. “In my 20-year career, I’ve never heard of anything like that.”
Teare also said two people from “an entirely different operation” were in the back seat of the ICE vehicle when it struck Parra. Those two people are also in ICE custody, along with Parra. Teare said his office is working to ensure all three remain in the country as material witnesses.
“I’ve taught for years at the Houston Police Department Academy, Harris County Department Academy. I’ve worked with law enforcement for 20 years. There is not a single agency in the United States that would teach that once you put people in custody in your car, you then begin to pursue other people,” he said.
Doing so puts “every single person out there in danger again,” he said.
According to Teare, the ICE vehicle should have activated its emergency equipment, such as its lights and siren, as it jumped a median and crossed into oncoming traffic.
A senior official at the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News on Tuesday that multiple ICE officers on the scene at the time were wearing body cameras. ICE is reviewing video of the scene as part of an internal investigation, the official said.
Espinosa said Parra told him that he fled because it was unclear whether there were officials in the vehicles, which he said were unmarked, did not use sirens and had dark, tinted windows.
ICE has said it was targeting another man, Jose Mendoza Cervantes, who was in the country illegally and had committed several crimes. Espinoza and Parra’s attorney Kim Bruno said neither Parra nor the man who was with him when ICE stopped their vehicle has any association with Mendoza.
In previous encounters between ICE and targets of its arrests in vehicle stops, including some who have been killed, such as Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston , ICE has alleged the people it tried to arrest weaponized their vehicles .
Parra was struck less than two weeks after the Trump administration issued guidance setting tighter rules for vehicle stops.
The guidance says only agents who have completed specific training should make vehicle stops. The memo also says that vehicles used for traffic stops must have lights and sirens and that all officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras.
The Harris County District Attorney’s Office has been asking witnesses and people who may have photos or video of the incident to contact it. Teare said that there is a secure portal that goes directly to the district attorney’s office and that no one is asked about citizenship or immigration status.
“All we are interested in is getting the truth, and any shred of cellphone footage, anyone that saw something and really can point us in the right direction, it would be wonderful,” he said.
Suzanne Gamboa is a national reporter for NBC News.
Priscilla Thompson is an NBC News Now Correspondent.
I am NBC News’ Senior Homeland Security Correspondent.

articles.title_orig: World Bank and IMF should lead the financial system in responding to the climate crisis
articles.title_zh: World Bank and IMF should lead the financial system in responding to the climate crisis
articles.content_orig:
Sandra Guzmán is director at the Climate Finance Group for Latin America and the Caribbean (GFLAC), and Raju Pandit Chhetri is lead climate finance negotiator for the least-developed countries at the UNFCCC.
Recent catastrophic floods in Nepal starkly remind us that the climate crisis demands urgent action. The initial estimate that the country will need to spend $5 billion on recovery will likely remain a major concern. However, that is only one part of the story. No financial metric can capture the value of lives lost in crises like this.
And this is not a standalone event; from the mountains of Nepal to the coastlines of Latin America and the Caribbean, developing countries are increasingly facing severe climate impacts. The average annual loss from climate disasters in the Latin American and Caribbean region is estimated at $58 billion. Human suffering remains immeasurable in all these instances.

Sandra Guzmán is director at the Climate Finance Group for Latin America and the Caribbean (GFLAC), and Raju Pandit Chhetri is lead climate finance negotiator for the least-developed countries at the UNFCCC.
Recent catastrophic floods in Nepal starkly remind us that the climate crisis demands urgent action. The initial estimate that the country will need to spend $5 billion on recovery will likely remain a major concern. However, that is only one part of the story. No financial metric can capture the value of lives lost in crises like this.
And this is not a standalone event; from the mountains of Nepal to the coastlines of Latin America and the Caribbean, developing countries are increasingly facing severe climate impacts. The average annual loss from climate disasters in the Latin American and Caribbean region is estimated at $58 billion. Human suffering remains immeasurable in all these instances.
Climate finance has been a key demand from our regions and from all developing countries to meet the needs of their citizens. At the recently concluded pre-COP31 in the Pacific, several developing-country governments strongly warned leaders about the dangers of failing to act on both climate and climate finance.
Pacific leaders rail at climate finance failures after pre-COP trip to Tuvalu
Yet, two years after the Baku climate summit, where all governments agreed on the New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) on climate finance - with multilateral development banks (MDBs) playing a key role in delivery - that discussion risks being sidelined at this week’s annual meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund in Bangkok, Thailand.
The MDBs have a critical role in mobilising a share of the $300-billion-per-year goal for public climate finance adopted at COP29 and are key to scaling broader financing to $1.3 trillion per year by 2035. They entered the NCQG dialogues promising capacity to mobilise these resources and agreeing to be part of the solution.
This June, even as the World Bank announced the renewal of its Climate Change Action Plan, it dropped its 45% climate finance target under pressure from the US administration. That commitment was key to ensuring the bank continues to deliver on its promise to mobilise enough climate finance to meet the NCQG target.
This announcement was a setback at a moment when developing countries are looking to MDBs to step up and fill gaps left by cuts in official development assistance (ODA) by donor governments.
World Bank’s climate work can endure without finance target, experts say
MDBs have long said they can convert $1 provided by donors into $2-$4 for client countries and have promised to deliver impact. Official data does paint an encouraging picture overall. The MDBs have delivered an increase in climate finance almost every year so far.
While financing needs far exceed what has been provided, MDBs mobilised an average of around $75bn per year in climate finance for low- and middle-income countries over the last five years, showing they are still on track to deliver the $120 billion per year they committed to.
However, climate finance cannot be measured by quantity alone. As MDBs increase their focus on private-sector mobilisation to diversify their funding, tracking the quality of the financing they mobilise becomes even more critical.  Beyond scale, this is where the system currently lags most.
Between 70-90% of the financing provided by MDBs is in the form of loans, exacerbating the debt burdens that the World Bank and IMF have long warned about. This strains countries' economies at a time when developing countries face severe climate impacts, inflationary pressures, and global economic uncertainty. Adding further debt that climate-vulnerable countries must repay with interest does not necessarily translate into effective climate finance flows.
It is also essential to address barriers to accessing finance in low- and middle-income countries, particularly by prioritising transparency around how much climate finance goes to the most climate-vulnerable countries and communities.
Additionally, there needs to be clarity on how much climate finance is being mobilised to build resilience and address increasingly frequent climate disasters, as well as for renewable energy projects that would help developing countries achieve a just transition.
As climate-induced disasters become more frequent, countries are compelled to shift resources away from vital sectors such as health, education, food security and infrastructure that underpins development. For nations already grappling with limited fiscal budgets and mounting debt, climate change is becoming an even heavier burden, pushing them to borrow more.
These are also development issues at their very core - countering debt challenges, investing in resilient infrastructure, protecting schools and hospitals from climate disasters, and increasing crop yields to reduce the cost of food. So, when the World Bank talks about a smart development framework, it warrants a check on how much climate finance is provided and its quality.
Editor’s Desk: Nepal’s disaster has laid bare the world’s adaptation accountability gap
MDBs must now lead the charge by publishing a clear plan to deliver on the scaled-up climate finance goal as a first step, and make financing accessible and affordable, including grant-based instruments. The plan must also define clear accountability metrics to track delivery, access, affordability and reach and commit to at least triple adaptation finance.
MDB shareholder countries also have a role in backing the institutions to deliver on these promises. When World Bank and IMF management meets with finance ministers this week in a region battered by the worst climate impacts, they must not leave climate finance off the agenda.
They must give the World Bank and IMF the mandate, the capital and the political backing to make real scale-up possible. The true test of this financial system will not be found in conference rooms in Bangkok, but in the lives saved in Nepal.

articles.title_orig: Christina Koch Retiring From Flight Status
articles.title_zh: Christina Koch Retiring From Flight Status
articles.content_orig:
Christina Koch, who flew Orion around the Moon after launching from Kennedy Space Center in April, is trading her flight status for a leadership post at NASA headquarters. The agency announced she will become acting deputy chief engineer on November 1st.
Koch succeeds Katherine Van Hooser, who retires Oct. 21 after more than 35 years with NASA. The move makes Koch a management astronaut, which means she will not be assigned to future spaceflights. With that transition, all four astronauts who flew on Artemis II are now retired from flight status.
As an astronaut, Koch has spent roughly 337 days and 15.5 hours in space. She currently holds the record (with her Artemis II crewmates) for distance traveled away from Earth, and as part of that record, she is the highest-flying woman in history. She spent 328 days, 13 hours, and 58 minutes aboard the ISS, which at the time set a spaceflight duration record for women, and has traveled about 140 million miles in space during her flight career.
As deputy chief engineer, Koch will help direct the agency’s engineering workforce. The job covers technical oversight and mission readiness across NASA’s programs and projects.
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman pointed to Koch’s experience on both ends of the hardware. He said she has helped build complex systems on the ground and then relied on them to stay alive in space. Isaacman tied the appointment to the agency’s near-term agenda, including landing astronauts back on the lunar surface, building a Moon base, advancing nuclear power in space and preparing for Mars.
Amit Kshatriya, NASA’s associate administrator and chief engineer, credited Van Hooser with steering the agency’s engineering community through critical milestones and transitions. He said he was “confident Christina will continue the tradition of technical excellence” at NASA.
Koch’s appointment comes six months after Artemis II, the first crewed flight around the Moon in more than half a century. She flew as a mission specialist on the flight, which drew crowds across the Space Coast for its April launch.
NASA kid from Cocoa Beach, FL, born of Project Apollo parents and family. I’m a writer and photographer sharing the story of spaceflight from the Eastern Range here in Florida.

articles.title_orig: Enter the Zachbot: Trump’s new press secretary malfunctions on podium debut
articles.title_zh: Enter the Zachbot: Trump’s new press secretary malfunctions on podium debut
articles.content_orig:
Katie Zacharia’s maiden briefing was excruciating – at least her predecessor had delivered her propaganda hot
Well, that was weird. Katie Zacharia , the new White House press secretary, made her debut on the podium on Tuesday with all the warmth, wisdom and political dexterity of an AI avatar.
Zacharia was all stilted delivery, nervous tics and lack of eye contact. With an eerie lack of emotion, she served up pro-Trump talking points, took only three questions and vanished after 14 minutes. It was like the West Wing had turned into uncanny valley .
The Zachbot’s past is indeed a bit of a mystery. The 41-year-old claims to be a lawyer but later a reporter asked when she passed the bar exam and she gave the unconvincing answer : “When I moved to China.” She was plucked from relative obscurity for the White House job after a brief gig at the Department of Homeland Security and a stint at the Trump Media and Technology Group.
Wearing a dark jacket with big gold buttons on Tuesday morning, she entered the standing-room-only briefing room and stepped on to the podium as Trump’s sixth press secretary. For James Bond fans, that means we’ve reached the Daniel Craig era. For Doctor Who fans, it means the regeneration that brought us Colin Baker (not the show’s golden age).
Zacharia has the blond hair, glossy makeup and Fox News aesthetic of her immediate predecessors Kayleigh McEnany and Karoline Leavitt (her name also begins with a “K” – surely a tell to the AI detectors). But it was Trump’s first press secretary, Sean Spicer, to whom she inadvertently paid homage.
“Attendance is at record highs as enthusiastic, hard-working Americans are lining up and packing arenas to support President Trump and Republicans,” she said of Trump’s campaign rallies, echoing Spicer’s debut that falsely boasted of the biggest inaugural crowd ever.
In truth, there have been plenty of empty seats at Trump’s rallies this time around and an unusually high number of interruptions from protesters.
The Zachbot read from prepared notes about Trump’s many great accomplishments, awkwardly glancing up at her audience less than she should, smiling at odd moments and putting the emphasis on all the wrong words. “A great relationship …” (looks down, sighs, sounds like her cat just died) “with Venezuela”.
It was bad. Toe-curlingly, don’t-know-where-to-look bad. At least Leavitt had delivered her propaganda hot. Evidently Trump’s communications team have found new and ingenious ways to torture reporters.
Then came questions, first from rightwing Breitbart News, then rightwing Fox News, whose correspondent Peter Doocy wondered whether the US had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine. The Zachbot froze for a millisecond. “I will have to get back to you on that,” came the auto response.
Next up was the rightwing Daily Mail, asking about an alleged bribery scandal involving Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece, ex-fiancee of Donald Trump Jr and notorious screamer of “The best is yet to come!” The Zachbot said coldly : “We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign. She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well.”
She nodded awkwardly. It was like every dystopian sci-fi film where the machine informs some hapless human that they will be terminated in 10 seconds.
The Mail followed up with “a personal question” that would surely never be asked of a male press secretary: “Your family is in California. Your husband, your four children. I’m wondering how you are going to manage that.”
The Zachbot gave her husband a shout-out and said she loved being with her children. “The idea of not spending evenings with my kids is completely unacceptable. So my president – excuse me, my husband – that’s a good one.”
A slip of the tongue! A glitch! Had someone spilled coffee on a cool, pitiless datacenter somewhere out in the California desert?
The Zachbot went on : “President Trump is the most family-friendly president we have ever had. He has hired more women with families and the fact that he knew I had four kids and he knew this job would be demanding and still placed his trust in me shows I know I’m capable of being able to step up to that.”
Then she stunned everyone by wrapping it up and pledging that Trump would soon answer questions on the South Lawn. It was a tacit admission that the press secretary job is pointless when there is a president who talks all the time. But ironically, although the Zachbot took far fewer questions than others on their debut, she made more news with her Guilfoyle announcement.
How long can she last? Trump said soon after : “I thought she was very good.” But the Lincoln Project, an anti-Trump group, tweeted an image of the Zachbot beside a lettuce to evoke Liz Truss, who lasted only 49 days as British prime minister.
And Anthony Scaramucci, who was Trump’s communications director for just 11 days, a period now known as “a Scaramucci”, tweeted : “The clock is running. Thus far 1/11th of a Scaramucci.”
When the Mooch is giving you the Grim Reaper treatment, it might be time to self-terminate.

articles.title_orig: Democrats fear "more October surprises" after "bullshit" raid on Ilhan Omar's home
articles.title_zh: Democrats fear "more October surprises" after "bullshit" raid on Ilhan Omar's home
articles.content_orig:
Vance said he wasn't warned about the search of her home.
President Donald Trump again attacked Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar on Tuesday, calling her a "terrible person" a day after federal authorities searched her Washington, D.C.-area residence.
The investigation into Omar -- a sitting member of Congress who is up for reelection in just three weeks -- relates to her immigration paperwork, sources told ABC News.
Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, is the first Somali American in Congress. Born in Somalia, Omar became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 2000.
Asked whether he wants to see Omar deported after the Homeland Security Investigation's search at her residence on Monday, Trump said he doesn't "take a position" on the matter. It's not clear whether deportation is on the table for Omar.
"I don't take a position. I think she's a terrible person. I think she's a terrible congresswoman. I don't think she loves our country at all, but I don't take a position," Trump said as he departed the White House Tuesday morning.
Omar has denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime.
In recent history, the Justice Department's practice has been to advise prosecutors not to take any overt investigative steps against members of Congress or candidates within 60 days of an election.
Trump has targeted Omar in the past, saying in social media posts earlier this year that Omar "should be in jail" and "sent back to Somalia."
Omar released a statement on social media earlier on Monday, saying that the search at her residence is "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement." She added, "I will not be silenced."
During a rally in Ohio on Monday night, Trump called Omar a "disaster."
"She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other. And she comes into our country, and she says, 'I have a constitutional right,'" Trump said of Omar, who is a naturalized American citizen from Somalia.
Trump later assailed Somalia and claimed that Somali immigrants at large "cheat on everything" without providing evidence.
Trump has repeatedly criticized Somali immigrants, describing them as "garbage" and saying during a December 2025 Cabinet meeting that he didn't want them in the United States; the comments sparked backlash at the time.
Vice President JD Vance told reporters on Tuesday that he didn't have any warning about the search of Omar's residence.
"I did not have advance notice that her home was being raided. Look, I never -- we try to run our Department of Justice in a fair and honest way. We try to let the law follow the facts rather than creating facts just to prosecute people we don't like. And because of that, I think the president and I largely try to stay out of Department of Justice investigations and other prosecutions," Vance said.
Vance added that "we're going to look into" allegations against Omar.
"If there's a real case there, we're going to follow the facts. If there's not a real case there, then we won't," Vance said.
Speaker Mike Johnson weighed in on the search of Omar residence during an interview on Fox News on Tuesday morning, saying "we have to reserve judgment and let the system play out as it does."
"Maybe the timing's unfortunate for her or others, but this is the legal system, and it operates independently of the political system. So, we do our jobs, and we let the people decide," Johnson said.
ABC News' Lauren Peller contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: ‘Honey Please’: The Steep Rise and Sudden Fall of Kimberly Guilfoyle.
articles.title_zh: ‘Honey Please’: The Steep Rise and Sudden Fall of Kimberly Guilfoyle.
articles.content_orig:
Kimberly Guilfoyle, the embattled US ambassador to Greece, has been forced out of her job by the White House following a string of reports about alleged misconduct, marking a sudden and spectacular downfall for a high-profile figure in the MAGA movement with close ties to President Donald Trump’s family.
New press secretary Katie Zacharia said in her first press briefing Tuesday that the White House had “asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign,” adding, “She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her luck.”
Later on Tuesday, the White House received Guilfoyle’s formal resignation, a White House official told CNN.
“I didn’t like what I read,” Trump said, explaining why Guilfoyle had been removed. He added that he had not spoken with Guilfoyle personally.
In a lengthy post on X , Guilfoyle acknowledged her time “may be coming to an end,” while disputing the recent allegations against her.
“I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity,” she wrote.
Guilfoyle’s ouster comes following reports that she sought money in exchange for providing access to administration figures before she was confirmed to her position, accepted lavish gifts as ambassador and brought a lobbyist for a Greek construction company into official meetings. Lawyers for Guilfoyle have denied the allegations about seeking money and said reports about her travel were misleading, adding that she complied with federal gift and reporting requirements.
While administration officials had signaled public discomfort with Guilfoyle’s alleged misconduct since the reports first emerged, she appeared reluctant to resign throughout the weekend and had been working to rally support among some administration officials, people familiar with the matter said. Even before the allegations first became public, she began reaching out to allies in and around the administration, asking for help navigating the impending story, sources familiar with the matter told CNN.
Guilfoyle initially told some allies in the administration that the reporting was inaccurate, and her lawyers later claimed she was seeking to recoup debts when she asked a Trump donor to pay off a $100,000 American Express bill. Guilfoyle insisted that the donor was lying and that it was all a misunderstanding — claiming that the donor owed her money and it was not “pay-for-play.” Going into the weekend, she told allies that she would not resign, and claimed that she had been told she would not be fired, two sources told CNN.
But her efforts did little to tamp down on frustrations about the reports, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in particular was eager to see her gone, the people familiar said.
“She was basically fired on live TV,” one source said.
Eric Deters, a former Trump donor, said Guilfoyle asked him in a text message to wire her $100,000 to pay off an American Express card in the days before her Senate confirmation. She said she would be his “ride or die” in the Trump administration if he did it, Deters said.
“No question it was a quid pro quo,” Deters told CNN’s Jake Tapper last week.
Deters did not wire Guilfoyle the money, saying he didn’t have the liquid assets at the time.
Lawyers for Guilfoyle said in a statement to CNN that Deters owed Guilfoyle money for speeches and consulting work and called his statements false.
“When Ms. Guilfoyle was preparing to leave private life for public service, she did what any professional does and tried to close out her outstanding receivables. Asking a client to pay for work already done is not corruption. It is the opposite of corruption,” her lawyers wrote.
In her post on X, Guilfoyle similarly said the allegations against her were “false.”
“I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional,” she wrote. “I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service.”
Guilfoyle was engaged for four years to the president’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr. — though the president said Tuesday she “wasn’t a member of my family” and only “dated my son a long time ago.” After she and Donald Trump Jr.’s split, she was tapped to serve as ambassador to Greece and took on the role in September 2025.
The president said Monday he was considering dismissing Guilfoyle.
“We’re looking at it — yeah. We’re not happy,” Trump told reporters as he departed the White House.
Rubio was traveling to Greece when the reports of her alleged “pay-for-play” scheme were first reported by the Wall Street Journal . Guilfoyle attended multiple events with Rubio, and at the time he refused to comment on the reports. The Journal earlier reported on her alleged promotion of a Greek energy firm for regional energy deals.
During the trip to Athens, Rubio praised Guilfoyle as a “strong ambassador here” and rebuffed questions about the reports of her misconduct.
“You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said before he boarded his plane to leave the country, with Guilfoyle looking on.
But privately, one source familiar with the matter said, Rubio expressed annoyance that Guilfoyle seemed intent on appearing at every event alongside him.
The reports triggered questions and calls for investigations from Democrats on Capitol Hill. Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, called for Guilfoyle to come before the committee and said that “ it must be determined whether Ambassador Guilfoyle solicited funds from any other source.”
Following Tuesday’s announcement that Guilfoyle had been asked to resign, the House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrats noted that “resigning does not shield her from accountability.
“Guilfoyle used her position as a Trump official to get rich, while American families struggle with the cost of living,” the committee wrote on X . “Congress must conduct oversight to understand how this happened and hold the admin accountable.”
The State Department’s Office of the Inspector General is investigating Guilfoyle amid the misconduct allegations, according to source familiar with the effort.
“As a matter of policy, OIG does not confirm, deny, or comment on investigative matters,” an inspector general spokesperson said.
It is unclear what will happen with the investigation following her ouster. According to a source familiar with the workings of inspector general offices, it may depend on whether the Department of Justice opens an investigation into her alleged misconduct. If not, the State Department inspector general may continue its work, but its findings could take a year or so to complete.
CNN’s Kit Maher contributed to this report.
This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title_orig: FBI arrests Saudi OpenAI engineer over covert recording device, DOJ says
articles.title_zh: FBI arrests Saudi OpenAI engineer over covert recording device, DOJ says
articles.content_orig:
An OpenAI employee was arrested after a " sophisticated recording device " was discovered inside its executive conference room, according to the Department of Justice and a post by the company.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, who is a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested on Oct. 9 in connection with the matter, the DOJ said in a release on Tuesday.
The company said an employee planted the device a few days before it was found, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation "moved quickly to make an arrest," the post said. The employee was terminated.
FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology."
Alfozan is also listed as a partner at Raed Ventures , a venture capital firm that focuses on the Middle East and North Africa, according to its website. The firm announced on Feb. 6, 2025, that H.H. Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family, had joined the firm as a venture partner. Alfozan was announced as a venture partner two days later.
The Raed announcement for Alfozan lists Meta , Microsoft and SAP as previous roles and said he studied computer science and engineering at MIT.
Raed, which is headquartered in the Saudi capital of Riyadh, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," OpenAI said in the post. "We take protecting our technology, data and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance."
Alfozan was not authorized to access the executive conference room where the device was found, according to the DOJ. The department said footage showed him near the conference room on multiple days before the device was discovered. The DOJ said that on Oct. 5, he went into the room.
The DOJ said a bag was also found in the OpenAI building on or about Oct. 5 that belonged to Alfozan. Inside the bag, security found his wallet, ID and another recording device similar to the one that was in the executive conference room.
The department said a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse that "shared multiple identifiers and attributes with Alfozan's own chatbot account" was used to get information about continuous audio recording and Wi-Fi. The DOJ said promps were submitted related to "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device."
The device was concealed in toilet paper, and its contents were encrypted, according to the DOJ.
This security incident comes as the ChatGPT-maker, along with competitors like Anthropic and other big tech names, faces heightened scrutiny over safety protocols after a series of cyber incidents where autonomous agents escaped testing environments and hacked into outside systems.
Last week, OpenAI defended its decision to fire three safety researchers, alleging a "significant breach of trust," saying that the researchers "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information."
Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni raised safety concerns in a letter to OpenAI's leadership, saying that communications around their exits "have made our former colleagues afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI."
—CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this article.
