articles.title_orig: U.K. intelligence chief warns Iran is shifting plots to ‘harder targets’
articles.title_zh: U.K. intelligence chief warns Iran is shifting plots to ‘harder targets’
articles.content_orig:
MI5 is devoting more resource to countering state threats than during the Cold War, the head of the intelligence service has said.
Sir Ken McCallum said threats from foreign adversaries had quadrupled in the last decade, with Russia "aggressor number one" as well as increased Iran-linked aggression against Jewish sites and military bases.
At an annual speech in London, MI5's chief said Russia was waging hybrid warfare at a time when AI was "supercharging the cyber-security contest between attackers and defenders".
He also warned of rising threats from "extreme right-wing terrorism" and said MI5 had "caught terrorists seeking to exploit AI," including by integrating the technology with drones.
He said the biggest threat from the misuse of AI was extremist groups using the technology to harness new and existing bioweapons.
However, he noted that work countering terrorism and state threats was now "pretty much of equal scale" which he described as a "huge shift" in recent years.
Sir Ken said Russia had stopped short of "conventional conflict" against Nato and is instead trying to unsettle European countries while its progress in its full-scale invasion of Ukraine is "minimal and horrifically costly".
Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.
These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.
Sir Ken said MI5 successes in identifying and expelling Russian spies from the UK had left the Kremlin dependent on paying proxies for attempted attacks.
"With its traditional covert footprint eviscerated by almost 1,000 expulsions since the invasion, the Kremlin's global toolkit is weak, he said.
"So we see them scrambling to pay criminals to do their bidding."
He added: "These are not the actions of a great power with the strategic upper hand."
His comments come as a growing number of leaders across Europe have warned Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine.
Asked after the speech about Prime Minister Andy Burnham's recent comments that Russia interfered with the Brexit referendum , Sir Ken said it was "not new news" that there had been attempts from Moscow but distinguished between "interference attempted" and "outcome achieved".
He said it was a matter of public record that there were pieces in Russian media and "so-called internet trolls and bot farms" seeking to influence the Brexit debate, but also stressed that the result of the 2016 referendum was "not in dispute".
He added that he was "worried" about the the ongoing debate on Russian interference.
"I am a little bit anxious that we don't play into our adversaries' hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall," he told reporters.
Meanwhile, Sir Ken warned that Iran is also expanding a hybrid campaign in the UK.
The intelligence chief said there had been 50 arrests in the last year over Iran-linked activities.
Much of this Iranian aggression has been aimed at Jewish communities, Sir Ken added, and also at "harder targets, like military sites".
Sir Ken did not mention arrests at RAF Fairford directly during his speech, but told reporters afterwards the incident was "not unique".
He added: "We have seen Iranian interest beyond RAF Fairford in the UK."
The incident at the airbase in Gloucesteshire, where three suspicious vans were seen parked nearby, has seen seven people arrested and bailed by counter-terrorism police.
Burnham has said the incident was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard".
The MI5 head said in his speech: "What I can say is that those who seek to cause mayhem on British streets - whether hired thugs here or their paymasters overseas - will meet an unflinching response."
Sir Ken added that the National Security Act - a 2023 law designed to target people working against UK interests for foreign powers - is in heavy use, and has been employed to tackle threats from China as well as Iran and Russia.
On the emerging threat posed by AI, Sir Ken said: "It can produce propaganda and radicalising material tailored to the individual.
"We've caught terrorists seeking to exploit Al to improve their reconnaissance and attack methodologies, with Al-enabled drones adding a new twist."
Sir Ken said the bioweapons threat posed by AI was "not yet realised" but warned the technology has the "potential to change the stakes".
"These risks are real. The UK Intelligence Community - MI5, GCHQ, MI6 - is working closely with the UK's globally respected AI Security Institute to take them on."
Sir Ken said AI poses unknown threats, telling Thames House: "Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are".
He announced MI5 had launched an AI Threat Assessment Centre, which he said would assess sources and "separate the bluster from the realities".
In April, the UK's terrorism threat level was raised to severe for the first time in five years, meaning an attack is highly likely.
Sir Ken said Islamist groups like Al Qaeda and so-called Islamic State both continue to direct and inspire attacks, while the increased risk was also driven "in significant part" by extreme right-wing terrorism.
He continued: "Over the last year the most marked trend has been an increase in cases where extremist versions of anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievance are tipping into terrorist intent."
Sir Ken said extreme right-wing terrorism tended to "skew young", driven by the internet - adding that MI5 had in recent months investigated a "radicalised extreme right-wing 13-year-old here in the UK".
He said: "That investigation generated insight that enabled one of our international partners to prevent a lethal attack on their soil."

articles.title_orig: Bipartisan group of senators call on Trump to rescind Russian diesel deal
articles.title_zh: Bipartisan group of senators call on Trump to rescind Russian diesel deal
articles.content_orig:
President Trump stops to speak to members of the media as he departs the White House on Oct. 13, 2026. Win McNamee/Getty Images hide caption
A bipartisan group of senators is calling on President Trump to rescind his recent diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, calling it a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine."
Last week, Trump announced via social media he had struck a deal with Putin, whereby Russia will supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and one million tons "immediately thereafter."
"Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Trump wrote.
His announcement stunned lawmakers, who passed legislation this summer directing the president to impose significant tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil.
Those sanctions are aimed at targeting Russian officials, companies and financial institutions helping fuel Russia's war in Ukraine. The legislation was named in memory of the late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham , who helped negotiate Trump's support for the package.
"This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies; it should be rescinded," wrote six Republican and six Democratic senators in a letter Tuesday to the president.
"The deal you struck with President Vladimir Putin on October 9 th will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," it read.
Senators said they recognized the need to lower energy costs for Americans — but maintained that allowing Russian diesel into global markets will offer "limited to no relief to Americans."
They added the deal "only provides Putin with more fuel to finance his war machine and enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians."
When asked about the letter, the White House referred back to comments President Trump made to reporters on Tuesday about concerns that Russia will use proceeds from the diesel agreement to purchase weapons.
"Nobody's telling me anything," Trump said. "That's a diesel deal. Not for us. That's being released into the world. That's not being released to us. That's a diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market, because the world market suffered with high prices."
The letter was signed by Democrats Richard Blumenthal, Chris Coons, Dick Durbin, Jack Reed, Jeanne Shaheen and Sheldon Whitehouse. They were joined by Republicans Alan Armstrong, Susan Collins, John Cornyn, Mitch McConnell, Lisa Murkowski and Thom Tillis.

articles.title_orig: World News in Brief: West African migrant crossings, Argentina takes UK to maritime tribunal, farming in Gaza, mental health update
articles.title_zh: World News in Brief: West African migrant crossings, Argentina takes UK to maritime tribunal, farming in Gaza, mental health update
articles.content_orig:
Facebook Twitter Print Email
Fewer people from West Africa are reaching Europe by sea, but the journey has not become safer, the UN migration agency (IOM) said on Tuesday .
Arrivals from Mali, Senegal, Guinea and The Gambia fell by 59 per cent in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, to 4,566 people.
But the drivers of migration persist. West Africans made up a growing share of arrivals on the Mediterranean routes, accounting for 21.9 per cent on the Western route, up from 15.6 per cent, pointing to a shifting landscape.
On the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands, arrivals fell 62 per cent between 2024 and 2025, yet recorded deaths and disappearances barely changed – 1,172 compared with 1,215.
Tighter controls in Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal are pushing departures south, adding up to 750 kilometres to crossings of around 2,200 km.
“No single country can solve this alone,” said IOM Director General Amy Pope. “We need to protect migrants wherever they are.”
Argentina has asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) to order the United Kingdom to halt an offshore oil project near the Falkland Islands (Malvinas), the Hamburg-based court said on Tuesday .
Buenos Aires wants the Sea Lion development in the North Malvinas Basin stopped while an arbitration case launched by Argentina on 28 September is under way.
It also wants London to refrain from steps that could aggravate the dispute, such as granting new permits.
A hearing date will be announced shortly.
The UN lists the Falkland Islands (Malvinas) as a non-self-governing territory and has long urged both sides to negotiate.
Britain has administered them since 1833; Argentina claims sovereignty and the two countries went to war over the islands in 1982. Buenos Aires seeks to resume bilateral negotiations over the islands.
London says the islanders have the right to determine their own future and no discussion over sovereignty can occur without their consent.
Tensions have risen in recent weeks, after President Javier Milei gave London a two-week ultimatum over the project, announcing tougher measures against any companies involved in oil and gas exploration around the islands.
Farmers in Gaza are facing increasing risks as they try to return to their fields.
In an update on Tuesday, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization ( FAO ), warned that the so-called Yellow Line of demarcation controlled by the Israeli military continues to expand into western Gaza.
This has increasingly limited access to agricultural land and prevented farmers from planting new crops.
FAO highlighted the case of 39-year-old grower Maryam, who described her small vegetable farm as a “lifeline” for her family of eight in southern Gaza.
Maryam is one of 1,700 farmers supported by FAO to purchase seeds, water and the other inputs they need to grow crops. The agency also helps herders and fishing families in Gaza
In her first season, Maryam harvested approximately three tonnes of okra.
“Farming is my life and my family’s life. It is the income source I depend on. Being able to farm again means that I am alive and that I can live with dignity with my family,” she told FAO.
There’s a new call from the UN World Health Organization ( WHO ) to reform mental health services by developing community-based models .
According to WHO, about half of all those living in psychiatric hospitals and other institutions around the world had no choice when they were admitted.
This is despite the fact that people living with mental health conditions “can flourish in their communities when given the right support”, the agency insisted.
Mark van Ommeren, Head of WHO’s Mental Health and Substance Use Unit, said large numbers in need of services “are forced to live beyond closed doors. About half were brought in against their will, stripped of basic daily choices like what to wear, when to eat and cut off from the outside world.”
Who said on Tuesday that many countries still rely heavily on psychiatric institutions and that across the world, nearly half of all public mental health funding is spent on maintaining them.
This leaves millions of people unable to get the care they need in general hospitals or in the community.
The WHO applauded Sri Lanka for replacing its isolated mental health institutions with community-based services.
Today, the country delivers care through inpatient and outpatient units in hospitals, clinics and rehabilitation units.
“When care is characterized by coercion, rigid control, or social isolation, it risks becoming a form of confinement rather than care,” WHO stressed.

articles.title_orig: Sizing up Meta’s push into the crowded world of enterprise AI
articles.title_zh: Sizing up Meta’s push into the crowded world of enterprise AI
articles.content_orig:
Meta’s plushy new homunculus wants to pull up a chair in your office.
As the Muse personal agent/cartoon mascot gains traction among consumers, Meta is also making a play for the crowded enterprise agent market.
Meta has hired former MongoDB CEO Chirantan “CJ” Desai to build out a new enterprise platform, as the company looks to provide services beyond advertising tools. It also announced a new Muse for Small Business tool that will integrate the agent into tools like Box, Figma, and Shopify, among many others. Details are vague right now on what an enterprise platform will look like, but Muse Code and Meta Business Agent will be among the already-existing offerings.
Business leaders and marketers we talked with said Muse shows computer use capabilities beyond those of other agents on the market, and could be more accessible to small and medium-sized businesses that already number among Meta’s advertising customers. But a wider enterprise play also comes with security concerns and wariness about Meta pulling in ever more data.
Meta is certainly not the first company to try to parlay consumer AI momentum into an enterprise product.
It might not be an obvious enterprise tech vendor in the same way as Big Tech rivals that boast cloud arms and office software suites. But Forrester principal analyst Kate Winick said the social platform company is already seen as a growth partner by the millions of businesses that use Meta Ads Manager. On that platform, Meta has been rolling out plenty of AI meant to speed or enhance the creative and audience targeting processes, to some mixed reactions from advertisers.
“The question of whether or not you personally trust Meta with your data is a different question than whether or not your company runs business through Meta,” Winick told us. “For most businesses, the answer is already yes. And so this allows [Meta] to sort of bring together the frontier model that they’ve built with the enterprise relationships they already have.”
But Meta Ads Manager is not without frustrations for some advertisers and agencies that use it regularly. For Jeremy Schulkin, SVP of services at marketing agency Hawke Media, there’s the problem of Meta “grading its own work.” Would Muse ever tell business users that their marketing money might be better spent on TikTok, for instance?
“We have fought hard to not hand over the keys to Meta,” he told us in an email. “Connecting QuickBooks, Stripe, your customer list, and your email gives Meta a full view of your business.”
Diego Lomanto, CMO at AI enterprise startup Writer (which would compete with Meta’s new platform), said Meta needs to demonstrate some form of “separation between church and state” between its consumer data-driven ads business and its enterprise platform in order to convince companies to trust it with their data.
Some companies that have experience with Meta’s agentic offerings have found them compelling, if sometimes limited.
Jack Johnston, VP of social innovation and growth at marketing firm Tinuiti, said the agency has piloted Meta’s model context protocol (MCP) server, which connects AI agents to advertising tools. He said the new agentic campaign manager in Muse for Small Business leans heavily on the MCP and is good for small businesses that might be unfamiliar with Meta ads.

“Comparing it to enterprise or SMB advertisers that already operate in Ads Manager, it can be a useful guide, but it lacks some of the sophistication that may be required,” he told us via email, adding that he expects Meta to add more sophistication as it moves beyond small businesses.
Kevin Gosschalk, founder and CEO of cybersecurity firm Arkose Labs, which also advertises on Meta platforms, said he’s found Muse to be far and away the best enterprise agent that he’s used, in terms of its computer use capabilities. That prowess is also evident in Arkose’s web data, he said, which shows more traffic on the web driven by Muse since it started to take off with consumers.
Arkose is currently having its security team review Muse for enterprise use, evaluating whether it would comply with the strict data requirements of client companies like financial institutions. He’s hoping that Meta eventually creates a version of Muse that it can host locally, like Meta’s latest models.
“Muse currently is a cloud-based service. So anything you give it goes into Meta’s data centers. That, we’re not able to do generally in a workforce environment,” Gosschalk said. “But Meta itself has a lot of businesses that use their platform—small businesses and things like that—where they don’t have those security requirements I’m describing. There’s a big divide between those kinds of businesses and a company like us that works with banks and stuff.”
Meta spokesperson Kamran Mumtaz pointed us to a blog post in which the company said it designed Muse to have “multiple layers of privacy and security protections.”
This new enterprise push isn’t Meta’s first attempt to sell workplace products beyond its core ads business. Since 2016, Meta had offered a communication platform called Workplace that was shuttered in May of this year.
“It was groups, it was internal messaging, and frankly, internal comms is a much lower priority for most businesses than growth and revenue,” Winick said. “This is targeted at a much more critical part of the business and working on much bigger problems than Workplace was ever intended to address.”
Still, it remains to be seen whether Meta can make a compelling case to businesses in a crowded space where its competitors have already spent years entrenching their own enterprise AI, Winick said.
“They’re going to have to make a strong case for why people need to switch or why the ad partner is the right person to build the overall business infrastructure,” she said. “They have relationships and they have a way in, but it’s not going to guarantee them the sale.”

articles.title_orig: Comments to the FCC on on Recommendations Approved by the World Radiocommunication Conference Advisor Committee - Information Technology and Innovation Foundation
articles.title_zh: Comments to the FCC on on Recommendations Approved by the World Radiocommunication Conference Advisor Committee - Information Technology and Innovation Foundation
articles.content_orig:
The Information Technology & Innovation Foundation (ITIF) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the World Radiocommunication Conference Advisory Committee’s draft recommendations regarding Article 22 equivalent power flux density (EPFD) limits under Agenda Item 9.2 at the 2027 World Radiocommunication Conference (WRC-27), with an eye toward fuller adoption of the FCC’s standards at WRC-31. [1] For purposes of Agenda Item 9.2, View A is the better step toward more productive use of satellite spectrum and would avoid unnecessary regulatory restraints that would limit the consumer benefits from non-geostationary orbit (NGSO) systems without significant benefit to geostationary (GSO) systems.
The rise of NGSO systems has been a major benefit to consumers as they now provide higher bandwidth and lower latency than GSO systems. While GSO operations still have important applications, regulations designed for a pre-NGSO world will artificially constrain the parallel benefits from NGSOs. The FCC has already taken the lead in updating domestic spectrum-sharing rules between NGSO and GSO systems, which will expand NGSO capacity, enhance consumer speeds, and provide more broadband to more people in more remote areas. [2] And the new rules do all this while allowing GSO operations to continue without significant degradation. These rules are a success story of updating regulations that would otherwise have held back the benefits of new technologies to those who can benefit from them most.
Thus, as the United States makes the case for this framework around the world, it should not go backwards by adopting a 100-percent-of-the-time EPFD limit, as proposed by View B, which would recreate unreasonable restrictions on NGSOs. The fundamental advance of the FCC’s updated sharing rules is to not guarantee certainty. View A’s unavailability criterion already limits the impact of interference events on GSO systems. An additional limit is unlikely to have an appreciable marginal benefit while the marginal cost could be large. View B would create a new limit not based on accepted technical anchors, which would not only substantially limit the consumer benefits of NGSO systems but would invite other countries to negotiate it to become even more restrictive.
Moreover, View A would adopt stringent protection criteria that protect GSO transmissions while removing unreasonably conservative EPFD limits that prevent NGSO operation even when doing so does not appreciably degrade GSO service. View B argues that View A insufficiently protects GSOs by, for example, lacking a 3-degree avoidance angle. View A, however, would still result in NGSO’s avoiding in-line geometry in practice. An NGSO system that cannot meet View A’s substantive protection of GSOs without avoidance angles will implement them. An NGSO system that can protect GSOs without avoidance angles would provide no additional benefit by bearing the cost of implementing them.
The benefits of NGSO systems are likely even greater in other countries than they are in the United States. For parts of the world without developed communications infrastructure, NGSO satellites promise high-speed, low-latency connectivity for the first time. The United States should, therefore, lead the way to maximize the benefits of NGSOs around the world and bring other countries along with it. It should not hamstring American satellite companies while also limiting consumer benefits of connectivity around the world. The United States should, therefore, support View A on Agenda Item 9.2 and reject View B.
Thank you for your consideration.
Joe Kane Director, Broadband and Spectrum Policy

articles.title_orig: 3,156-pound pumpkin grown in Rhode Island is inspected for possible world record
articles.title_zh: 3,156-pound pumpkin grown in Rhode Island is inspected for possible world record
articles.content_orig:
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
HALF MOON BAY, Calif. (AP) — A Rhode Island pumpkin grower appears to have broken the world record for the heaviest pumpkin, with his giant squash topping the current record by nearly 300 pounds (136 kilograms).
Ron Wallace of Greene, Rhode Island, weighed his pumpkin Saturday at a contest in New England and is now waiting for the Guinness Book of World Records to confirm he smashed the record, set about a week earlier by a grower in England. Wallace said he’s been in contact with Guinness officials who say his record is on track to be verified.
“It’s truly massive, it was a pleasure to grow,” Wallace said Monday by phone.
The Guinness Book of World Records currently lists a 2,857-pound (1,296-kilogram) squash grown by Ian Paton, of Lymington, England, as the record holder, set on Oct. 3.
Guinness officials did not respond to a request for comment.
The record-breaking gourd comes as growers across the world are joining competitions this month in the hopes their pumpkins will be crowned king. In Northern California on Monday, a Minnesota grower won a prominent annual competition for the fifth time in a row.
Wallace went home with $3,500 at his local contest. He said other competitions tried to entice him with bigger prize money, some totaling $70,000, but it was important for him to be surrounded by his hometown for the record-setting win.
“I was just ecstatic, the place just exploded,” Wallace said, describing the moment the pumpkin was weighed.
Wallace says he owes a lot to the pumpkin-growing community who always freely share tips and tricks to grow the biggest gourd. For the first time this year, Wallace began growing his pumpkins in a greenhouse, which he says makes a big difference.
“The only way you create a 3,000-pound pumpkin is a community working together,” he said.
Wallace got into the hobby after starting his own business selling gardening supplies online. He’s proud to be a part of the pumpkin-growing community and says competitions help legitimize growers. According to Wallace, the agriculture industry is increasingly reaching out to pumpkin-growers, asking for advice on soil and other growing techniques.
In Northern California, a pumpkin named Rocky won a major annual pumpkin-weighing contest, tipping the scale at 2,389 pounds (1,083 kilograms), but fell far short of a possible new world record.
Horticulture teacher Travis Gienger hauled his pumpkin across the country from Minnesota to win the contest for a fifth time. He’s going home with $21,501 in prize money after beating dozens of other giant pumpkin-growers in Half Moon Bay, south of San Francisco.
He missed out on last year’s contest because his pumpkin broke while growing. Hoping for a comeback story, he named this year’s pumpkin “Rocky” after the iconic boxer played by Sylvester Stallone.
“Five-time champion, that’s what we came here to do,” Gienger said following the win.
Gienger and his family drove 35 hours, lugging a pumpkin the size of a small car, to California.
Gienger grows his gourds in his backyard pumpkin patch in Anoka, a city on the banks of the Mississippi River north of Minneapolis, according to Ronan Fowler, the competition’s organizer. This year, Gienger had to deal with temperatures that dipped below freezing, and he says that in order to start competing more seriously, he’ll likely have to start growing pumpkins in a climate-controlled environment like Wallace.
“The fact that Travis can weather the elements, like 30-degree weather, and still grow this massive pumpkin is pretty unbelievable,” Fowler said.
Hundreds attended the 53rd World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off to enjoy food trucks, music, and pumpkin-related jokes. Earlier in the day, the crowd went wild when a very symmetrical pumpkin named Tinkerbell won the prettiest pumpkin contest.
The prize money was calculated at $9 per pound of pumpkin, and Gienger’s winning gourd will be showcased during a parade through Half Moon Bay this weekend. Gienger missed out on an extra prize of $30,000 for breaking the world record.
Sadly, these giants are grown for their size, not flavor, so there were no giant pumpkin pies at the end of the festival.
Associated Press writer Olga R. Rodriguez in San Francisco contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Cornell University bans frat parties, vows to address 'disturbing' campus culture
articles.title_zh: Cornell University bans frat parties, vows to address 'disturbing' campus culture
articles.content_orig:
Fraternities on Cornell's campus will not be allowed to host parties or events for the rest of the academic year. Jeongyoon Han for NPR hide caption
Cornell University has banned parties and social events at fraternities for the rest of the school year and will bring sexual assault investigators into its police unit, in response to a former student's allegation of gang rape in 2024.
The changes came on Tuesday as the university said it is committed to addressing a "deeply disturbing" culture of drug and alcohol abuse, and a rise in sexual violence on campus following a civil lawsuit filed by a former student, Jane Doe, which set off national outrage and a crisis at Cornell.
"I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community," Michael I. Kotlikoff, who is Cornell's president, wrote in a letter addressed to the campus on Tuesday. "It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action."
The lawsuit, which Doe filed nearly one month ago, alleges that Doe was plied with ketamine and was sexually assaulted by members of the Chi Phi fraternity during a party in October of 2024. The details of the allegations, which disclosed how fraternity members used a Snapchat group chat to discuss the woman and events at the party with openly crude language, sparked fury across the nation.
Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, told news outlets that Doe has been sent death threats and police swarmed her family's home since she filed the lawsuit.
The administration's changes come after student groups organized protests last week on campus.
"The administration is clearly feeling the heat and needed to make a move," says John Hartnett, a sophomore at Cornell who has helped organize protests. He called the changes a "half measure," and said that banning frats was not a long term solution to systematic issues at the university.
The faculty senate is considering a vote of no confidence in the university administration at a meeting scheduled for Wednesday. It's a rare move that demonstrates the deep seated frustration and distrust stemming from the 2024 case.
"Trust is still eroded on campus — that hasn't changed," says Julia Chang, an associate professor of Hispanic studies in the Department of Romance Studies. "The fact that these changes are coming about now — two years later — is a testament to the power of the student movement and the global conversation it has sparked; not the integrity of the administration."
The moratorium on events at fraternities is expected to have a reverberating effect on campus, where about one-third of all students participate in fraternities and sororities. The university's ties to Greek life, Kotlikoff said, has in part created a toxic culture on campus that requires serious course correction.
"While this is not a problem unique to Cornell, we are committed to setting a higher standard for education, oversight, and enforcement of safe social behavior and citizenship," Kotlikoff wrote.
Ray Epstein, who works with a consent education company, and is one of the organizers of a rally planned just steps away from Cornell's campus on Tuesday, said that while the measures from Cornell are "overall a win," they also serve as an "effort to save face."
"What I think they should be doing, is operating first instead of as a business, the way that they are now, as institutions that are meant to educate and keep their students safe," Epstein said.
Kotlikoff said that in addition to enhancing bystander training programming, the university will also improve its services to survivors of sexual assault by increasing staffing in its civil rights office, which would help individuals navigate the reporting process for incidents.
Additionally, the university will work with the New York State Police's criminal investigators on campus sexual assault investigations. The move allows the investigators, who are independent from the university, to take on cases in which survivors pursue criminal charges.
The university plans to bring in faculty who are experts in sexual assault and rape culture to help reform the Presidential Task Force on Sexual Assault through listening events with the Cornell community.
Kotlikoff's letter did not explain why these events are only being issued now — two years after administrators at Cornell learned about the allegations in 2024.
Although the district attorney did not prosecute the case in 2024, Cornell's Title IX office conducted an investigation in 2025. In March 2025, a panel of staff and faculty at Cornell moved to expel or suspend some of the men. The panel required the remaining men to write "essays" in addition to other sanctions.
Cornell also barred the Chi Phi fraternity chapter, which was closed in 2024.

articles.title_orig: One of the World’s Largest Chinstrap Penguin Colonies Is Shrinking Fast
articles.title_zh: One of the World’s Largest Chinstrap Penguin Colonies Is Shrinking Fast
articles.content_orig:
Scientists are sounding the alarm after discovering that one of the world’s largest chinstrap penguin populations has collapsed.
Zavodovski Island, a remote, uninhabited volcanic island between South America and Antarctica, lost 63 percent of its chinstrap penguins between 2011 and 2025, according to a new study published October 7 in the journal Current Biology .
Researchers attribute the losses—which amount to half a million breeding individuals—to climate change, which they say is disrupting the birds’ food supply.
“Imagine losing 60 percent of a country’s entire population in that timeframe,” Lucas Krüger García , an ecologist with the Chilean Antarctic Institute who was not involved with the research, tells National Geographic ’s Avery Schuyler Nunn. “It’s really concerning. The fact that this single colony represented 30 percent of the global chinstrap population makes it even more concerning.”
Zavodovski Island, part of the South Sandwich Islands , was once home to the largest penguin colony on the planet, a combination of chinstrap and macaroni penguins. But, since 2011, as chinstrap numbers have plummeted, the island has lost more than a quarter of its total penguin population. Because of the declines, scientists say the island has now lost its world’s largest penguin colony title to the Adélie penguins living at Cape Adare in Antarctica’s Ross Sea.
Chinstrap penguins have been declining across the Antarctic Peninsula and surrounding islands since the 1980s. But, for years, the birds living on Zavodovski Island, located some 1,240 miles from the nearest permanent human settlement, appeared to be holding their own.
In December 2023, scientists decided to check in on the Zavodovski chinstraps. They were in for a shock: Their analysis—conducted using a combination of drone surveys, aerial photography and satellite tracking data from individual birds—revealed that the island now has the highest rate of chinstrap population decline in the world.
In 2011, scientists counted nearly 543,000 breeding pairs of chinstrap penguins on the island. By 2025, that number had plummeted to roughly 201,000 breeding pairs, according to the paper.
The team ruled out a variety of explanations for the birds’ demise. The island has plenty of breeding habitat, so the chinstraps likely weren’t competing with their macaroni neighbors for space. Krill harvesting is banned in the waters surrounding the island, which eliminated local overfishing as a culprit. The March 2016 eruption of the island's Mount Curry might have killed some of the birds, but it doesn’t explain the chinstrap population’s steady decline since 2011.
Instead, the evidence points to climate-driven changes to the Southern Ocean that are affecting krill , the tiny crustaceans that make up the bulk of the chinstrap penguins’ diet. As the ocean warms and sea ice shrinks, krill are becoming increasingly scarce around Zavodovski—and chinstrap penguins are paying the price.
Tracking data shows the birds prefer to forage in the cooler waters northwest of the island, where they would normally find abundant krill. However, as ocean temperatures rise, the krill are increasingly moving south into the Weddell Sea .
Since chinstrap penguins rely so heavily on krill, even small changes in its availability can have significant consequences for their survival. The chinstrap penguin is “quite a specialist species that’s got a very limited global range, and that range is getting squeezed,” lead author Norman Ratcliffe , an ecologist with the British Antarctic Survey, tells CNN ’s Laura Paddison.
Did you know? Emperor penguins are also in trouble
Earlier this year, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) listed emperor penguins as “endangered.” Projections suggest the birds’ population could shrink by as much as half by the 2080s.
Meanwhile, the island’s macaroni penguins are holding steady. The birds’ numbers increased by 28 percent between 2011 and 2016, and have remained stable at roughly 217,000 breeding pairs since then. Zavodovski Island now has a combined chinstrap and macaroni penguin population of roughly 419,000 pairs, per the paper.
Scientists think macaroni penguins are faring better than chinstraps because their diet is broader and more flexible. They also like to eat krill, but can supplement with or switch to other food sources, such as fish and crustaceans, when necessary. Tracking data suggests they’re doing just that, heading to the warmer waters northeast of the island to forage for alternate prey.
Overall, it’s good news that Zavodovski’s macaroni penguins are flourishing. But researchers worry that the decline of chinstrap penguins could have broader ripple effects.
“Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set, and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely,” Ratcliffe tells the Guardian ’s Jonathan Watts.
Sarah Kuta is a writer and editor based in Longmont, Colorado. She covers history, science, travel, food and beverage, sustainability, economics and other topics.

articles.title_orig: Bank earnings: Higher rates haven't hurt consumer spending or AI financing, yet
articles.title_zh: Bank earnings: Higher rates haven't hurt consumer spending or AI financing, yet
articles.content_orig:
Four of the largest U.S. banks reported third-quarter results on Tuesday: JPMorgan Chase , Wells Fargo , Goldman Sachs and Citigroup .
Bank of America and Morgan Stanley will post earnings on Wednesday.
The quarter was dominated by headlines around artificial intelligence, IPO uncertainty, high fuel prices and rising borrowing costs.
The banks that reported Tuesday put up mixed results . JPMorgan, the biggest U.S. bank by assets and the largest in the world by market capitalization, posted a rare miss. Goldman Sachs, meanwhile, blew past estimates for revenue and earnings per share, led by strong equities trading.
Analyst calls for all four banks touched on the opportunities and risks associated with AI, citing robust financing demand and operational advantages, but also the threat of rogue agents.
Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon also addressed recent reports of a CEO transition plan, and Wells Fargo CFO Mike Santomassimo joined CNBC to discuss the firm's growth and the state of the consumer.
Here's what you need to know:
Citi's analyst call is over, which means bank earnings reports for Tuesday are wrapped. Bank of America and Morgan Stanley report on Wednesday to round out third-quarter results for the major U.S. firms.
Wells Fargo's Santomassimo told CNBC that both consumers and businesses are doing "really well."
"I think despite higher gas prices, both sides of the equation have been able to really work through that," he said. "We're just not seeing any sort of cracks around delinquency trends that would lead you to believe you're going to see any near-term stress that come through, at least at least for now."
Wells Fargo CFO Mike Santomassimo told CNBC's Sara Eisen that the company's underlying results are "really good" and that the bank is seeing "continued momentum" across all of its businesses.
"As you look at the net interest margin, what that really shows is sort of this good stabilization of the underlying trends," he said. "You see the higher rate environment starting to come through in terms of helping it as you look forward, and so for us, the opportunity we have ahead of us is just as big as it was last quarter."
Citi's Fraser said on the call with analysts that macro environment conditions softened during the third quarter and that the "global economy has held up remarkably well."
"In the U.S., while much has been made of the AI boom, the consumer is still driving much of the growth," she said. "The labor market is stable, and companies remain active. Our near-term economic outlook remains positive."
She added that the bank's clients have remained "engaged" and "healthy."
Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser said on a call with analysts on Tuesday that the company is focused on reducing systemic risk while deploying AI firmwide.
"Our cyberdefense strategy is about being on the front foot, about moving fast and retaining trust," Fraser said. "We don't wait for risks to happen. We're constantly preparing and improving our defenses. We're in the business of managing risk everyday, and this is no different."
Investment banking fees at all four firms reporting on Tuesday largely held up during the third quarter, with most firms either matching or surpassing prior guidance. Still, the reports revealed declines on a quarter-over-quarter basis.
At JPMorgan, investment banking revenue was up 14% year over year but down 8% quarter over quarter. JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said the pipeline remains "very, very strong."
Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon echoed that sentiment on his company's analyst call, while declining to say whether capital markets activity has peaked. That bank reported fees that were 21% higher from the prior year, but 5% lower than the second quarter.
"IPOs that came in September were really the result of conversations in May and June around valuation expectations. Things got a little bit softer in September," Solomon said. "The IPO market was wide open. It's just if you expected a valuation and you got something 10 %to 15% less, you might choose not to go forward, you might choose to wait."
Solomon added all the tech innovation and the AI infrastructure activity is a "real good ballast" for capital markets activity on a go-forward basis, noting that doesn't mean there won't be bumps.
Citi posted the largest quarter-over-quarter decline in the fees, at 13% down. Wells Fargo reported investment banking revenue that was down 5% from the prior quarter.
Solomon warned that the AI infrastructure boom could face a painful reset if higher borrowing costs or overbuilding undermine the economics of some data center projects.
"There is going to be a lot of financing to do, and we're going to be in the middle of that," Solomon said during the bank's third-quarter call.
"It may be that over time as the financing needs grow, that there's pressure on rates and that will affect the returns and the viability of certain projects," he said. "Not every project is going to be received as well."
For now, demand for computing power remains strong and supply has yet to catch up, Solomon said, meaning more infrastructure will be built and more financing from Goldman and others will be needed. It's impossible to predict when a reset might happen or how the technology would evolve and be deployed, he said, calling the dynamic "an unknown we have to live with."
"There will be a point in time when this recalibration resets, for sure," Solomon said. "When that does happen, of course there'll be some bumps."
Citigroup, the final bank of the morning, is beginning its conference call with executives and analysts to discuss its third-quarter earnings results.
Goldman Sachs CEO Solomon pushed back against reports of an impending transition to executive chairman, saying Tuesday that no succession process or timeline is underway at the investment bank.
Last month, news outlets cited anonymous sources that said Solomon would be replaced as CEO by Goldman President John Waldron as early as next year. The process would involve a vote by the bank's board that could happen in a matter of months, according to The Wall Street Journal.
"I just want to be clear, there is no succession transition or timeline underway at Goldman Sachs," Solomon said during the bank's earnings call.
"The board and I are singularly focused on our strategy to grow the firm and continue to serve our clients," he said.
The CEO also pointed to the firm's future growth prospects, saying his leadership team was focused on expanding the franchise and accelerating its earnings growth in the coming years.
"I have to say, at the point right now where we see the benefits of the effort that the broad team has made, I'm really enjoying the job," Solomon said.
Wells Fargo's Scharf said on the call with analysts that the AI investment cycle has become "a complicated macroeconomic force in its own right."
"Demand for semiconductors, networking equipment, power generation, data center infrastructure, cooling systems, storage, cybersecurity and advanced manufacturing equipment continue to surge," Scharf said.
"The scale of investment here increasingly resembles prior infrastructure booms, creating both significant opportunities but also risks given the significant leverage used to finance the build-out and the upward pressure on prices in selected industries and supply chains," he added.
Scharf said on the call with analysts that the company's customer base is "still strong."
"Our underwriting criteria recognize that at some point consumer credit conditions will weaken," Scharf said. "To be clear, we do not see signs of this yet, but we know that cycles are inevitable."
Wells Fargo's Scharf said on the call with analysts that the company is "devoting significant management time and resources" to building out its AI capabilities.

articles.title_orig: Investigators hunt French supermarket fridge hackers, no claim of responsibility
articles.title_zh: Investigators hunt French supermarket fridge hackers, no claim of responsibility
articles.content_orig:
Hackers targeted hundreds of French supermarkets in a cyberattack that reportedly caused refrigerators and freezers to overheat, spoiling food and sparking fires.
Fridges at French supermarket chains Carrefour, Monoprix, the Les Mousquetaires-owned Intermarché, and Coopérative U, among others, all saw fridges heat up to as much as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) overnight, Reuters reported Monday.
Coopérative U's CEO, Dominique Schelcher, confirmed that cyberattacks had affected "refrigeration production facilities of several stores."
"Attacking equipment that is essential to the preservation of fresh products and the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and unprecedented. It is unacceptable," Schelcher said in a LinkedIn post .
CNBC has reached out to Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarché, Coopérative U and E Leclerc for comment but did not immediately hear back.
Felix Aime, a senior cyberthreat intelligence analyst ​at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, said the attack affected several European countries, including Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium, according to the Reuters article.
"I strongly condemn the cyberattack targeting food products at @intermarche @CooperativeU @Leclerc," European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Christophe Hansen said in a post on X on Monday.
"Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponization of food has become a reality."
Les Mousquetaires said it was expecting the damages, which affected around 180 stores, to reach "several million euros in losses," in an email to CNBC.
It said some fresh and frozen food displays have been out of service after the cyberattack affected one of its service providers responsible for managing refrigeration systems inside some stores.
"Intermarché and Netto have taken all necessary precautions to remove and dispose of any affected products as quickly as possible, to ensure consumer safety," the Les Mousquetaires spokesperson said. "In some stores, the overheating of equipment resulted in smoke, but no fires have been reported."
They're now awaiting findings from a court-appointed bailiff and insurance experts to get more precise figures on damages.
Stop & Shop parent Ahold Delhaize , which owns popular Dutch supermarket chain Albert Heijn, said that it was experiencing a "security issue within its network," and that systems had been taken offline. It said its stores are still open.
This comes amid a broader wave of cyberattacks and cybercrimes, which experts are warning are being enhanced by artificial intelligence. British online fashion retailer Asos experienced a cybersecurity breach last week which revealed some customers' personal information.
Meanwhile, a small power plant in the U.K. was shut down for four days in July after a cyberattack which was suspected to be linked to Iran.
Interpol's global chief information security officer, Bjorn R. Watne, recently told CNBC that AI can be used to target multiple victims at once, and is increasing the scale and speed of cyberattacks. "It's an evolution and not a revolution."
Correction: Bjorn R. Watne is global chief information security officer at Interpol. An earlier version misspelled his name.

articles.title_orig: Op-Ed: Transparency Alone Won't Deter China in the South China Sea
articles.title_zh: Op-Ed: Transparency Alone Won't Deter China in the South China Sea
articles.content_orig:
By The Lowy Interpreter 2026-10-13 15:15:55
[By Charmaine Misalucha-Willoughby]
On 10 October, the National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea (NTF-WPS) reported that 22 vessels from the Chinese maritime militia had been deployed near Kota Island, a Philippine-held area in Palawan. The task force also confirmed that Chinese Maritime Militia Vessel 9622, along with 22 small boats, returned to the area after two weeks, where they engaged in unauthorised fishing and dumping waste at sea.
A few days prior, on 8 October, a China Coast Guard (CCG) vessel used water cannons on a Philippine medical mission to evacuate a Filipino soldier from the BRP Sierra Madre in Ayungin Shoal. The BRP Sierra Madre is the Philippine vessel purposely grounded in Ayungin in 1999, in response to China’s militarisation of a nearby reef (Mischief Reef).
The Philippines and China signed a “provisional understanding” in 2024 to provide both sides with a predictable process and reduce the risk of miscalculation. Despite this, the Philippines confirmed on 25 September that the CCG and the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) obstructed a rotation-and-resupply mission to the BRP Sierra Madre. Another Philippine vessel, the BRP Datu Magat Salamat, sustained damage on 18 September after a CCG ship rammed it while en route to deliver fuel to Filipino fisherfolk.
These incidents support the Philippines’ observation that China’s military and coast guard presence in the West Philippine Sea doubled in the last month. The Philippines monitored 101 PLAN and CCG ships around Pag-Asa Island, Ayungin Shoal, Escoda Shoal, and Chinese-controlled Scarborough Shoal. That number is almost double the 56 vessels recorded in August 2026.
Repeated intrusions and coercive action at sea are practically a staple in China’s tool chest in the South China Sea. Beyond these, however, widespread malign information campaigns on maritime issues in the West Philippine Sea challenge national security narratives and public trust in democratic institutions. Chinese messaging includes rewriting history, undermining the Philippines’ independence, and projecting a positive image through development projects. This approach gives China access to economic channels through elite influence and capture.
At the recent Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said that the country is “resigned” to managing tensions with China and avoiding escalation. The stance is far from that of acquiescence. Indeed, the Philippines’ transparency approach replaces the previous policy of quiet diplomacy with public documentation and exposure of coercive maritime actions. Under the initiative, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) and the NTF-WPS actively publicise videos, photos, and reports of Chinese activities in the West Philippine Sea. By shifting attention to public exposure, the objective is to raise domestic awareness and combat disinformation campaigns. Likewise, the Philippines hopes to garner further international support for upholding the 2016 arbitration award.
While Filipinos generally view the approach positively, it is not a strategy on its own. The ultimate test is whether this transparency approach has changed China’s behaviour so far. The number of incidents and coercive manoeuvres in the last month alone indicates that the Philippines must level up its game.
Beyond transparency, the Philippines can also do the following. The Marcos Jr. administration’s Comprehensive Archipelagic Defence Concept (CADC) laid the groundwork for substantive changes to Philippine military strategy by emphasising basing dispersion, ranged strike capabilities, and the use of geography. Because it could be seen as a “counter” anti-access/area-denial strategy to China’s posture, especially given the Philippines’ expansion of military positions near Taiwan, Manila needs to deepen its foreign military partnerships and integrate them into the archipelagic concept. Doing so would mean stating clear positions on basing access, weapons deployments, and in-theatre assets. Previous plans largely avoided these conversations to preserve strategic flexibility. However, now is the time to jump-start these discussions, which would require developing not only a theory of victory but also an effective strategic communications plan to translate strategic-level deterrence efforts into tactical and operational effect.
Second, the transparency approach is one way of combating foreign information manipulation and interference, but building situational awareness and exposure is only one step in a series of moves. The Philippines must coordinate messaging and actions around shared values, the national interest, and its red lines. It must learn – fast – to hold the semantic high ground. Words may be cheap, but words are the building blocks of narratives and discourses on which people’s identities are rooted and flourish. Alongside coordinating messaging and actions, the Philippines can work with partners and allies to strengthen digital regulations and tech accountability, given that most Filipinos rely on Facebook for news and information. Indeed, the country is considered the world's social media capital. Pushing for tech accountability must include private entities and state-backed or proxy media outlets to foster social and institutional resilience. These efforts can drive cooperation at various levels.
Finally, the Philippines should make the most of its 2026 Chairmanship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). Although the year is almost over and the agenda and deliverables are already set, the Philippines must show its willingness to turn ASEAN from a mere convening platform into one with normative power. While ASEAN managed to bring in extra-regional powers and preserve the so-called long peace in Southeast Asia, that no longer holds true today. Without a solid response to Myanmar, the Thai-Cambodia border, or the South China Sea, the regional organisation will inevitably lose the centrality it holds dear. The norms on which ASEAN has stood since its inception – consensus and non-interference – reflected the realities of 1967, which are not necessarily the same today. As the 2026 ASEAN Chair, the Philippines should lead the discussions on the region’s normative gains. This can help revamp the organisation and update it to reflect today’s dynamics.

articles.title_orig: World stocks slip as AI spending worries hit chipmakers
articles.title_zh: World stocks slip as AI spending worries hit chipmakers
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Sruthi Shankar and Chibuike Oguh
NEW YORK, Oct 13 (Reuters) - World stocks edged lower on Tuesday as concerns about AI spending weighed on chipmakers and investors looked ahead to more US corporate earnings for clues on whether big technology ‌firms can justify their heavy capital spending.
Brent crude futures also fell as traders assessed developments in the Middle East ‌conflict.
Investors have ridden the AI wave in the past four years as massive spending powered corporate profits and economic growth, but more recently, worries over concentration risks ​and whether a payoff will come soon enough have weighed.
On Wall Street, all three indexes finished lower with industrials, healthcare, and financials driving losses. Chip stocks lost more than 2%.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.35%, the S&P 500 fell 0.02% and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.15%.
The pan-European STOXX 600 index fell 0.1%. MSCI's main world stocks index dipped 0.23%.
"The AI trade has been driving the market for the first ‌part of the year up until the third ⁠quarter and usually the Nvidias and AMDs trade down ahead of the hyperscalers' earnings announcements because of the uncertainty with regards to the capital spending cycle," said Gerry Sparrow, president and portfolio manager at ⁠Sparrow Capital Management.
Reported progress by Chinese memory chip maker CXMT has fueled concerns about increased competition from China's AI players, while Broadcom CEO Hock Tan likened some of the flows into the broader AI sector to "casino gambling."
Investors are turning their eyes to the US quarterly earnings season, which ​kicked off ​with results from big banks.
Shares in JPMorgan Chase dropped 0.86% after it ​reported a profit increase in the third quarter, driven ‌by investment banking and trading performances. Wells Fargo dropped 3.1% and Goldman Sachs fell 0.23% after their results.
AI heavyweights Alphabet, Amazon.com, Meta Platforms and Nvidia are yet to report their quarterly earnings.
"Until we get clarity on hyperscaler capital spending and revenue on the AI trade, you're going to see some very mixed results on the benchmarks: Dow, S&P 500 and the Nasdaq," Sparrow said.
The benchmark 10-year yield fell 2.72 basis points to 5.22%, inching away from the 24-year high of 5.364% it hit last week.
A toxic ‌mix of inflationary pressure from elevated energy prices and worries about ballooning ​government debt has triggered several bond selloffs in recent weeks, pushing borrowing costs to ​multi-decade highs across the globe.
Traders are awaiting US inflation data ​on Wednesday for clues on the Federal Reserve's policy path. They are pricing in an 80.6% chance ‌that it holds rates steady later this month, up ​from 51% a month earlier, the ​CME FedWatch tool showed.
Oil prices eased as traders assessed supply risks from attacks on Saudi Arabia while weighing the prospect of additional diesel supplies from Russia. Brent crude futures dipped 0.9% to $105.69 per barrel.
The dollar slipped from 18-month highs, along ​with a drop in yields and oil prices. ‌The euro was last up 0.01% at $1.1199, while the Japanese yen was at 158.31 per dollar. [FRX/]
The dollar index, which ​measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, fell 0.34%.
(Reporting by Chibuike ​Oguh in New York; Editing by Will Dunham and Jamie Freed)

The career grand slam winner, who has earned well over $200 million on the golf course alone, has entered into a global partnership with DP World. articles.title_orig: After Bangkok Floods, IMF and World Bank Weigh Global Risks
articles.title_zh: After Bangkok Floods, IMF and World Bank Weigh Global Risks
articles.content_orig:
Home Features After Bangkok Floods, IMF and World Bank Weigh Global Risks
Author: Paul Curcio |
		Photos: 		Shutterstock
IMF and World Bank's annual meeting explores economic resilience amid climate risk, debt pressure, and AI.
While walking around central Bangkok, it’s easy to miss the damage that prompted IMF and World Bank officials at their annual meeting to consider postponing this week’s event.
No evidence of the extreme flooding elsewhere in the city, which caused so much damage and loss of life just a week ago, is visible. Life goes on—scooters buzz and trucks barrel down the expressways and narrow streets where vendors hawk exotic foods and trinkets. Bangkok officials did an admirable job cleaning up to prepare for the arrival of some 15,000 attendees, and the area surrounding the convention center is as dry—and secure—as it’s probably ever been.
Inside the meetings, though, the question was how much more disruption—climate-related or otherwise—the global economy can absorb, and who can afford to recover when the next shock arrives.
At Tuesday’s World Economic Outlook briefing, IMF Chief Economist Silvana Tenreyro described a world economy being pulled in two directions. Conflict in the Middle East has pushed energy prices higher, while investment in artificial intelligence has helped drive growth. The IMF outlook projects global growth of 3.1% this year, but that headline figure masks sharp differences among countries. Energy exporters and countries driving the AI boom are better positioned, she said, than those that must import fuel or have little stake in the massive technology surge.
“The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits,” Tenreyro said at the briefing.
The economy is holding up, in part, because countries and companies have navigated disruptions by rerouting supplies, drawing down inventories, improving efficiency, and finding alternatives. Without those adjustments, the IMF estimates global growth would be closer to 2.5%.
But these measures have limits. Inventories run down. Efficiency gains can only go so far. And another shock—whether geopolitical or climate-related—could arrive before economies have recovered from the last one.
The Intergovernmental Group of Twenty-Four on International Monetary Affairs and Development, or G-24, which represents emerging-market and developing economies, brought the issue closer to home. Nigeria’s finance minister and G-24 chair, Taiwo Oyedele, cited the flooding in Thailand to argue that climate commitments need to be backed by money, not just promises.
“Our appeal to world leaders is to put their money where their mouth is,” he said in a separate briefing shortly after WEO’s.
For businesses, resilience has a price. Holding extra inventory, diversifying suppliers, and keeping cash on hand can seem like unnecessary costs when markets are stable. But during a disruption, they can keep production moving and prevent higher costs from affecting the business.
Countries face a similar trade-off but lack the same resources. Developing economies need funding for infrastructure, climate preparedness, and basic services, even as debt payments consume a large share of public funds. Oyedele cited estimates that developing countries pay roughly $500 billion more in debt costs than developed economies. His broader point is clear: The countries that need to invest in resilience often face the highest financing costs.
Iyabo Masha, director and head of the Secretariat of the G-24, described the dilemma this way: “Debt is something that restrains growth.” When governments spend so much on creditors, she said, they have less left to invest in their economies.
Another uncertainty in the IMF’s outlook is that AI investment may boost growth, but its benefits do not necessarily translate into jobs. Oyedele warned that countries with younger populations could see growth alongside rising unemployment if they do not plan carefully. Growth, he said, “has to be job rich; it has to be inclusive.”
That’s a broad definition of resilience—not simply keeping an economy growing, but ensuring people benefit and that governments retain the capacity to respond when circumstances change.
In Bangkok, the discussions have ranged from growth forecasts to debt and climate finance. But the underlying question is who can afford to prepare for the next disruption and who will be left to pay for recovery.
Central Bangkok shows little sign of the recent flooding, but that doesn’t mean the damage elsewhere was any less severe. The same holds for the global economy: A resilient growth forecast doesn’t mean every country is equally prepared for the next shock. The question is how much each can afford to absorb—and what it might have to give up to recover.
Paul Curcio is the editor of Global Finance Magazine. Contact him at paul.curcio@gfmag.com.

articles.title_orig: ‘Super app’ aimed at UK students uses servers owned by Chinese firm on US blacklist
articles.title_zh: ‘Super app’ aimed at UK students uses servers owned by Chinese firm on US blacklist
articles.content_orig:
ZyMix platform has contract with Tencent, which US alleges has links to People’s Liberation Army
A new messaging and payment “super app” marketed at British students uses servers owned by a Chinese company that has been put on a US military blacklist for its alleged affiliation to the People’s Liberation Army.
ZyMix, which is being pushed on university campuses as the UK’s first super app designed “for gen Z”, combining chat, payments and community features, has a contract with a German-based subsidiary of Tencent Holdings, a Chinese conglomerate in Shenzhen.
Tencent Holdings was added in January 2026 to the US Department of Defense’s (DoD) list of Chinese military companies, which is formally known as the section 1260H list.
The citation on the DoD list says that the company, which is a gaming and social media conglomerate, is indirectly affiliated to the Chinese People’s Liberation Army.
The blacklist is part of a US attempt to counteract what it regards as Beijing’s efforts to increase its military power by using technology from Chinese firms, universities and research programmes.
The DoD is prohibited from entering into, renewing or extending contracts for goods, services or technology with any entity on the list although wider sanctions are not automatic.
A Tencent spokesperson said: “Tencent’s inclusion on this list is clearly a mistake. We are not a military company or supplier. Unlike sanctions or export controls, this listing has no impact on our business. We will nonetheless work with the Department of Defense to address any misunderstanding.”
China’s footprint in higher education in the UK has become a controversial issue. MI5 recently warned British universities to cut ties with the China General Technology Research Institute.
The domestic intelligence service claimed it was secretly channelling funding from Beijing’s intelligence apparatus to UK-linked academics to improve the technical espionage capabilities of China’s ministry of state security.
The link between the Chinese-owned infrastructure and ZyMix was initially disclosed in the company’s privacy policy at the time of its launch last week.
The document, which is legally required, said that Tencent (Frankfurt) stored user-generated content and messages. After the Guardian approached the company, the privacy policy was rewritten and mention of Tencent was removed.
The policy now states that users’ personal data is stored and processed primarily in the United Kingdom and the EU, adding that “some of our service providers are located in other countries, including the United States”.
It goes on to say that “auxiliary infrastructure providers, hosted in the EU, receive only encrypted user messages and limited technical data, such as technical statistics, licence validation when the app starts”.
A spokesperson said: “As a newly launched startup, we are updating our privacy notice as we develop our services, including clarifying that Tencent, Twilio and the other providers concerned are used solely for performance testing.”
The spokesperson added: “Our agreement is with Tencent Cloud Europe BV, which we use for auxiliary services, rather than as the provider that stores ZyMix user data. We take our obligations under UK data protection law seriously.”
The new privacy policy invites those who wish to know the identity of their suppliers to request the information from the company.
In response to a request from the Guardian, Tarique Ghaffur, a former assistant commissioner at the Metropolitan police, who described himself as a security consultant for ZyMix, responded.
He said: “We have reviewed your request as against our private privacy [sic] you mentioned. Unfortunately, at the present time for reasons of commercial confidentiality, contractual obligations and legal privileges, we are not able to provide you with the requested information.”
Fraser Sampson, a professor of security and national governance and formerly the UK’s biometrics and surveillance camera commissioner, said he was “sceptical when ‘commercial confidentiality’ arguments are used to duck basic policy questions and amending policy on the fly is never reassuring”.
He added: “When companies ask us for our personal data, they should expect us to ask them where it’s being kept, for what purpose(s) and who they’re going to share it with – and be prepared to answer fully.”
Sam Dunning, the director of the UK-China Transparency NGO, said: “There are serious questions about whether ZyMix have taken due care before launching this product.”
A spokesperson for ZyMix said: “Whilst still in its beta stage, the ZyMix app has been developed to fully comply with all UK data, privacy and financial regulations.”
ZyMix is heavily targeting the university market and is offering £200 to £400 a month to people who agree to be brand ambassadors on campuses. Staff roles have also been advertised in the UK by ZyMix for Mandarin-speaking applicants.
One advert on LinkedIn for the job of operations manager (Mandarin speaking) required “excellent written and verbal communication skills in both English and Mandarin (required for daily communication with the China team)”.
Separately, a distinct company appeared to be recruiting on behalf of ZyMix on WeChat, the Chinese instant messaging service, saying: “The product, R&D, design and testing team is in Greater China, with branch-company bases covering: Taipei / Shenzhen / Guangzhou / Hangzhou / Chengdu / Zhengzhou.”
Ghaffur said that Flicknmix, the UK company that publishes the ZyMix app, “does not have any subsidiaries or branch offices in China. Our aim is to create opportunities within the UK”. A spokesperson for ZyMix described it as “British born”.

articles.title_orig: The Forces Driving Up Bond Yields Take a Troubling Turn
articles.title_zh: The Forces Driving Up Bond Yields Take a Troubling Turn
articles.content_orig:
The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell on Thursday as traders digested comments from a top Federal Reserve official along with another long-dated bond auction.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was down more than 4 basis points at 5.229% after reaching its highest level since 2002 this week. The 30-year Treasury bond yield dropped more than 5 basis points to 5.602% after trading around a 24-year high recently.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Thursday that more hikes are needed to bring inflation down after around 5-and-a-half years above the central bank's 2% target, but suggested rates did not need to rise immediately.
"The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings," Waller told a Central Bank of Turkey forum in Istanbul. "But they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."
His comments initially sent yields higher on the day. However, rates gave back those advances after President Donald Trump said the U.S. won't attack Iran until after the November midterm election . Yields also pulled back after a solid 30-year Treasury bond auction.
The department sold $22 billion in 30-year paper, with indirect bidders — which include central banks — scooping up 72.3% of the sale. That's above a 10-auction average of 68%. Direct bidders, including institutional investors, took 20.9% of the auction, just below an average of 22%. The yield at auction ease 5.618%.
That marks the final auction of the week. The department sold $58 billion in 3-year notes on Tuesday and another $39 billion in 10-year notes.
Thursday's sale "was decent but nowhere close to as good as the 10 yr auction yesterday," wrote Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer of One Point BFG Wealth Partners.
— CNBC's Brianna Bernath contributed reporting.
