articles.title_orig: He Would Be Florida’s First Black Governor. Can He Sway Black Voters?
articles.title_zh: He Would Be Florida’s First Black Governor. Can He Sway Black Voters?
articles.content_orig:
Undecided Black voters, David Jolly says, may decide who becomes Florida’s next governor.
Appearing in Tallahassee Monday, Jolly and running mate Gwen Graham were flanked by U.S. Rep. James Clyburn, a South Carolina Democrat, and former Democratic U.S. Rep. Al Lawson of Tallahassee, both prominent Black political figures.
About 10% of Black voters are undecided, Jolly said, with about 80% of siding with him. An NBC 6 poll shows Jolly with 76% of Black voters’ support and U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds , a Black Republican, with 10%.
“I think there are two final fronts in this race,” Jolly said, one being “the disaffected Republican.”
Donalds is “trying to scare a lot of Republicans to come back home,” Jolly continued.
“But I would say the most important front that this entire race could come down to is the 10% of undecided Black voters in Florida right now. We are around just north of 80 [percent], which historically three weeks out is about where we should be as a Democrat. Byron’s at about 9 or 10 [percent]. And the final front and the voters that might decide this race are the currently undecided Black voters in the state of Florida.”
If elected governor, Donalds would be the first Black governor in Florida’s history. Yet, per polls, Black voters seem to be siding with the Democratic candidate, who is white.
“Someone said to me, ‘Are you concerned, Jolly as a Democrat, you’re only getting about 80-81% of the Black voters,’ and I said, ‘Not as concerned as Byron should be that he’s only getting 9% of his own community. But that last 10% is where I think this race could get decided,” Jolly said.
Jolly on Monday met with the Florida State University Black Student Union and Divine Nine sorority and fraternity chapter leaders at FSU and Florida A&M University.
Angie Nixon, a Black Florida House member from Jacksonville, as the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate “helps a lot,” Jolly said.
“One of the comments I have made and I’ve continued to make, look, there will be voters who decide to reach for history in this race. Some will reach for history because they want to elect the first Black governor. I don’t argue with that; if that is what is informing a voter, it’s not my place to argue with them,” Jolly said.
“I don’t squabble with the reach for history. That’s not my place to do. I do squabble with the agenda and the platform, and I think Byron has a hard time justifying his candidacy to a lot of communities, including the Black community.”
He pointed to those advising his campaign. Rev. Dr. R.B. Holmes, a Black minister in Tallahassee is chair of a coalition of pastors from historically Black congregations supporting Jolly, and various Black state legislators are part of his leadership team.
The former representative Lawson — who lost his seat when Florida’s Republican governor and Legislature dismantled his minority-opportunity district — insisted Jolly would make Florida history, too.
“A vote for Jolly is a vote to change the course of Florida,” Lawson said.
Meanwhile, at a FAMU town hall Jolly answered questions from the audience, which included students. He was pressed on immigration, healthcare, and education.
As a fifth-generation Floridian, Jolly said he was aware of the significance of FAMU, the state’s only public HBCU, but acknowledged no one in his family had experienced campus life there.
He did note the time under former FAMU President Frederick Humphries when FAMU successfully recruited more National Achievement Scholars — once a National Merit Scholarship recognition and financial award for high-performing Black high school students — than Harvard.
But the Legislature never rewarded FAMU for its accomplishments, Jolly said.
As governor, Jolly said he’d settle a lawsuit filed by FAMU students in 2022 that alleges, among other things, the state systemically underfunded the campus by nearly $2 billion over the past three decades.
“We could let the court settle it or we could settle it in the Legislature right now,” Jolly said.
A student asked Jolly how, as a former member of the Republican Party, he could assure the “Black diaspora” that he “won’t be like those that came before you and what will you do on Day One to prove to us of your intentions?”
Jolly initially replied, “Is this where we pull the fire alarm?”
It was a reference to his Republican opponent’s appearance at a FAMU town hall two weeks earlier. That event was interrupted when a fire alarm went, off requiring the auditorium to be vacated. After about a 40-minute delay, Donalds resumed his town hall.
Jolly’s remark was met with laughter from the crowd and even a bit of applause. Then Jolly said:
“Let me follow up with this. I don’t think the problem is that I used to be a Republican. I think the problem is my opponent still is a Republican.”
This story has been updated to include Jolly’s remarks a a FAMU Town Hall Monday night.

articles.title_orig: Utah’s ‘world’s longest art gallery’ could see 500 oil trucks a day. A new lawsuit aims to stop that.
articles.title_zh: Utah’s ‘world’s longest art gallery’ could see 500 oil trucks a day. A new lawsuit aims to stop that.
articles.content_orig:
(Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance) Gate Canyon with a winding dirt road that would be straighten and paved under a plan approved by the Bureau of Land Management.
Note to readers • This story is made possible through a partnership between The Salt Lake Tribune and Grist , a nonprofit environmental media organization.
Environmental groups are suing the federal government over plans to blast a “ hydrocarbon highway ” through a Utah canyon full of cultural, archaeological and historical resources.
The Trump administration resurrected the project in Nine Mile Canyon in eastern Utah after it stalled out during President Joe Biden’s term. Environmental and historic preservation groups say approvals for the highway bypassed the normal public comment and ecological review processes. The Nine Mile Canyon Coalition, Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance and Center for Biological Diversity filed a lawsuit against the Department of Interior and Bureau of Land Management on Oct. 6 to stop the project.
“It’s like constructing a highway through the Louvre Museum,” J. Michael Hansen, president of the Nine Mile Canyon Coalition, said in a statement.
(Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance) A Native American rock art panel in Nine Mile Canyon near Price.
The BLM’s website refers to Nine Mile as the “world’s longest art gallery” due to its extensive ancient petroglyphs, Native American panels and Pioneer-era axle-grease inscriptions. Nine Mile Canyon covers about 46 miles, and Gate Canyon has 47 historic sites with 43 eligible for the National Register of Historic Places, according to BLM documentation from 2015.
A BLM spokesperson declined to comment on the lawsuit.
The federal agency began considering plans to realign Gate Canyon’s winding dirt Wells Draw Road in 2015. Duchesne County sought a more direct route from the oil fields in the Uinta Basin to the rail facilities of Carbon County. The project could bring up to 500 heavy trucks through Nine Mile Canyon per day . Duchesne County has also said straightening the old county road would provide for safer travel.
In 2016, the BLM received nearly 700 public comments sharing concerns about impacts to Nine Mile Canyon from the increased traffic, the agency noted in its latest assessment.
The proposed highway would run 5.3 miles through lands owned by both the Bureau of Land Management and Utah’s Trust Lands Administration, although most of the switchbacks the highway project would straighten occur on state land.
(Bureau of Land Management) A proposed realignment of Wells Draw Road that would create a "hydrocarbon highway" between the oilfields of the Uinta Basin and the rail facilities of Carbon County.
The BLM paused its earlier environmental assessment of the project, the lawsuit claims, but it solicited public comments again in 2023 after reviewing an amended right-of-way that covers 2.8 miles running through federal lands. The highway proposal was again hit by a round of opposition. The plan was scrapped, with BLM citing the need for further cultural surveys and reports.
But a Duchesne County special service district submitted a new development plan in September 2025, which they finalized on April 13 of this year. The BLM approved it on April 28 after determining the highway “will not significantly affect” the environment, recreation, wildlife or quality of life.
In their lawsuit , the environmental groups disagreed with that assessment.
“The road construction will facilitate increased traffic through Gate Canyon and the adjoining Nine Mile Canyon, threatening some of the state’s most important cultural and scenic values in the larger Nine Mile Canyon region,” the lawsuit said.
Although the BLM issued a final environmental assessment in April, the environmental groups said the agency violated several federal laws, including the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act, the Federal Land Policy and Management Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.
The Gate Canyon project area potentially includes habitat for the threatened Mexican spotted owl, according to the agency’s own 2015 draft environmental assessment, environmental groups argued.
And despite that previous draft assessment identifying dozens of sites within Gate Canyon that are eligible for the National Register, including 11 “within feet” of the existing dirt road, the parties say the BLM signed off on the project without identifying any historical or archaeological resources.
The plaintiffs said they asked for public comment periods and to participate in the NEPA process after learning of the highway’s new development plan in March, but that the BLM either did not respond or denied those requests.
“This lawsuit challenges the Trump administration’s disgraceful plan to transform a quiet backcountry road into a highway clogged with speeding oil tanker trucks,” said Deeda Seed, senior Utah campaigner at the Center for Biological Diversity. “We’re going to court to protect this irreplaceable cultural treasure and the animals calling it home.”
The federal government has not yet filed a response with the Utah District Court.

articles.title_orig: Leap seconds have righted global clocks 27 times. So why do timekeepers want to kill it?
articles.title_zh: Leap seconds have righted global clocks 27 times. So why do timekeepers want to kill it?
articles.content_orig:
When the sun hits its highest point over the meridian line that travels north and south from the 351-year-old Royal Observatory Greenwich in London, it’s noon Greenwich Mean Time, a tangible and physical reference point that helped establish the world’s time zone system.
Timekeeping has long relied on Earth’s spin and location of the sun or moon in the sky. Before observatories such as Greenwich, humans used sundials — essentially a stick in the ground that casts shadows as the sun moves overhead. But this ancient link between Mother Earth and today’s clocks looks set to be severed.
Stonehenge was an ancient time-keeping system, archaeologist says
International timekeepers are on track to vote Thursday on a proposal to eliminate what’s known as a leap second — a tiny, but many say important, link between Earth’s rotation and the world’s time standard used in critical infrastructure such as telecommunications, power grids and computers.
Inserted into global clocks 27 times since 1972 , the leap second essentially allows two time systems to run in sync: astronomical time, long anchored by Earth’s rotation and measured by observatories, and Coordinated Universal Time, or UTC, the global standard that’s set by ultraprecise atomic clocks first developed in the 1950s. These cutting-edge, lab-based clocks rely on tracking the natural vibrations — or ticks — of atoms.
The two time-telling methods differ because Earth does not rotate at a steady pace but wobbles, essentially making it a “lousy” clock, said Jeff Sherman, a group leader of the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Time and Frequency Division in Boulder, Colorado.
This wobbling stems from various factors, such as the moon’s gravitational pull, shifts deep in the planetary core, and the movement of water and ice on Earth’s surface — an effect that’s exacerbated by the melting of the polar ice caps due to the climate crisis.
“We have to make a choice on whether or not the most important thing is a sense of time given by objects in the sky directly above, say, the Greenwich longitude,” he said referring to the Greenwich meridian that marks 0 degrees longitude. “Or you decide to follow what you believe are more stable, laboratory, man-made clocks,” Sherman added.
Leap seconds have served as the compromise between the two time-telling systems. Most people never notice them — unlike a leap year , which adds an extra day to February every four years to account for the discrepancy between the Gregorian calendar used in most parts of the world and the time it takes Earth to complete one orbit around the sun.
But the addition of leap seconds, which happens at irregular intervals and is announced with only six months’ notice, creates problems for operators of data servers, high-frequency financial trading systems and other infrastructure that rely on precise timekeeping to work properly.
The extra second crashed Reddit and LinkedIn and knocked out Qantas’ booking system in 2012. And when the most recent leap second was added at the end of 2016, customers of cloud computing provider Cloudflare briefly experienced outages or delays after its servers failed to handle the introduction of a leap second properly. Big tech players such as Meta have been calling for its demise, describing the leap second as “a major source of pain.”
The 69 member states of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, an intergovernmental organization that determines measurement standards, will meet this week in Versailles near Paris. The group, known by its French acronym BIPM, will vote on a resolution to ditch the leap second, a move that would take effect in May 2027. A majority needs to support the proposal, said Patrizia Tavella, director of the time department at BIPM.
When atomic time was first introduced, Tavella said, it was important to keep it tethered to astronomical time because navigational tools still relied on traditional celestial methods and timekeeping. With the advent of GPS, however, that was no longer the case. “This correction in time has become a serious issue for modern applications,” she added.
Why scientists say we need to send clocks to the moon — soon
Members of BIPM have discussed the switch to what Tavella called Continuous Coordinated Universal Time for more than 20 years, she noted. At the group’s last meeting in 2022, member countries voted in favor of a resolution that called for a plan to phase out the leap second on or before 2035.
In the past, some countries, such as Russia and the United Kingdom, have opposed ditching the leap second, she noted. Russia’s 2022 opposition stemmed from the fact that its Global Navigation Satellite System, or GLONASS, incorporates leap seconds, unlike other satellite navigation systems, such as the United States’ GPS and the European Union’s Galileo, that do not. The United Kingdom was once opposed because of its cultural attachment to the foundational role that Greenwich played in the history of time, but its stance has since changed, she added.
Since the world’s timekeepers last met in 2022, the debate over whether to abolish the leap second has taken on an urgency because of the prospect of something unprecedented: It will soon be necessary to subtract rather than add one second, known as a negative leap second, according to experts.
The long-term trend of Earth’s rotation is slowing, but in the near term it appears to be speeding up, potentially requiring a subtraction of a second from Coordinated Universal Time to keep astronomical and atomic time matching.
A 2025 report by the International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service, a consortium headquartered in Frankfurt, Germany, tasked with tracking Earth’s rotation, estimated that the likelihood of a negative leap second would rise sharply in the coming years — hitting a probability of 30% by 2035, according to BIPM.
Deleting a second has never previously been attempted and could create havoc in today’s digitally time-stamped world. BIPM said the operators of critical infrastructure are “largely unprepared” for such a move. “The preparation would create, for the industries that rely on time synchronization, a need for financial investment, whose amount is estimated to be similar to their preparations for the millennium bug,” the organization said, referring to Y2K, a computer flaw that programmers thought might cause severe systemic problems after December 31, 1999.
However, not everyone agrees that it’s necessary to ditch the leap second.
The technical challenges of incorporating leap seconds, whether negative or positive, into digital systems were overstated, according to Marek Ziebart, a professor of space geodesy at University College London who said there was value in keeping the world’s fundamental timescale aligned with Earth’s rotation.
“We have a system in place that uses leap seconds. It works. It maintains the timescale that all of us use on a day-to-day basis,” Ziebart said. “If you abolish the leap second, a lot of things will have to change. People will have to check their software, redesign it, fix it.”
He added that it was also “intellectually comforting” to maintain a timescale tied to Earth’s rotation. “There’s an intrinsic relationship for human beings between rotation and time,” he said. “It relates to us as animals. We’re driven by these periodicities of the sun rising, the sun setting.”
Instead of juggling positive and negative leap seconds, the BIPM resolution essentially proposes that atomic time would be allowed to drift gradually away from astronomical time. Doing so means official timekeeping would become independent of Earth’s rotation, and another leap second would never be added to clocks.
However, the proposal does recommend that the maximum difference between atomic and astronomical time should not exceed 3,600 seconds or one hour. It would take more than 3,000 years for such a difference to occur, BIPM’s Tavella said.

articles.title_orig: James Webb reveals a massive cosmic structure that challenges our understanding of the Universe
articles.title_zh: James Webb reveals a massive cosmic structure that challenges our understanding of the Universe
articles.content_orig:
A massive galaxy cluster dating back to an era when such enormous structures were only beginning to take shape is challenging scientists' understanding of how the universe evolved. New observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) reveal that the cluster contains an unusually dense concentration of matter, suggesting that some cosmic structures may have developed much faster than current models predict.
The galaxy cluster, known as XLSSC 122, has become the focus of three recent studies led by researchers at IPAC, Caltech's science and data center for astrophysics and planetary science. Their findings establish XLSSC 122 as the most distant galaxy cluster known to exhibit strong gravitational lensing, a phenomenon that allows astronomers to measure the mass of otherwise invisible matter. The research was presented at a press conference on June 17, 2026, during the 248th meeting of the American Astronomical Society.
Located approximately 10.4 billion light-years from Earth, XLSSC 122 stood out to astronomers because of its surprising maturity. Although it existed during a period when galaxy clusters were still assembling, it already displayed the size and organized structure typically associated with clusters in the modern universe.
Webb has now uncovered another remarkable feature. XLSSC 122 happens to lie directly in front of one or more galaxies that are even farther away. The cluster's powerful gravity bends and distorts the light traveling from those background galaxies, creating a rare effect called strong gravitational lensing. This fortunate alignment has given scientists an exceptionally precise way to measure how mass is distributed throughout the cluster.
"When we got those first images back from JWST, we said, 'wow, look at this, there's strong lensing coming from this cluster!'" said Kyle Finner, a staff scientist at IPAC and lead author of the first paper examining the cluster. "XLSSC 122 has now set the record for the most distant galaxy cluster displaying strong lensing, which is a valuable tool for astronomers."
An Ancient Galaxy Cluster Challenges Cosmic Predictions
The newly detected gravitational lensing has allowed researchers to examine the distribution of mass in an ancient galaxy cluster in greater detail than ever before. XLSSC 122 dates to a period known as "cosmic noon," roughly 10 billion years ago, when the universe was experiencing its most intense era of star formation.
During this time, galaxies were producing stars at rates up to 100 times higher than those observed in the present-day universe. Galaxy clusters were also becoming increasingly common as smaller systems gradually combined into larger structures.
Yet XLSSC 122 appears to have developed in an unexpected way. The new measurements show that a remarkably large amount of its mass is packed into its central region. According to standard cosmological models, the growth of massive structures should have been more gradual, making such a concentrated cluster particularly surprising at this early stage of cosmic history.
"XLSSC 122 is one of the first clusters we know of that formed in the universe, and it has a mass concentration that doesn't agree with our cosmological model predictions," said Finner.
To investigate the mystery further, Finner and his collaborators conducted two additional JWST studies, first authored by Zachary Scofield and Hyungjin Joo at Yonsei University. Together, the three papers provide a much more complete picture of this unusual cluster and offer new insights into galaxy cluster formation during cosmic noon.
James Webb Reveals Hidden Dark Matter
Astronomers originally identified XLSSC 122 in 2014 through an X-ray survey carried out by the European Space Agency's XMM-Newton spacecraft. Later observations with the Hubble Space Telescope helped establish its distance of approximately 10.4 billion light-years and confirmed that the cluster appeared unusually developed for its age.
However, Hubble did not reveal clear evidence of strong gravitational lensing. That changed when JWST captured distinctive curved arcs of light surrounding the cluster's center, providing the first definitive signs of this phenomenon in XLSSC 122.
"Before JWST, we couldn't do this level of science in the early, distant universe," said Finner.
The gravitational distortions are caused primarily by something astronomers cannot directly observe: dark matter.
Although XLSSC 122 contains visible stars and glowing gas, these familiar forms of matter account for only a small fraction of the gravitational lensing effect. Most of the distortion comes from dark matter, an invisible substance that has not been directly detected through light but whose gravitational influence is supported by extensive astronomical evidence.
Scientists estimate that dark matter is approximately five times more abundant than ordinary matter, which makes up stars, planets, and everything around us. Its gravity helps hold galaxies together and shapes the universe's enormous network of galaxy groups, clusters, and filaments.
Because dark matter plays such an important role in cosmic structure, determining how it was distributed billions of years ago offers a powerful way to test theories describing the universe's development since the Big Bang approximately 13.8 billion years ago.
"Strong lensing is a way to measure the dark matter without actually seeing the dark matter," said Finner. "It gives us a sensitive probe of our cosmological models."
A Wider View Reveals a Galaxy Cluster Merger
In their second paper, the researchers investigated XLSSC 122 using another form of gravitational lensing known as weak lensing.
Strong gravitational lensing produces obvious distortions, including the striking arcs captured by JWST. Weak lensing, by comparison, causes much smaller changes in the apparent shapes of distant galaxies. These subtle effects are difficult to identify individually, so astronomers rely on statistical methods to detect them.
The two techniques provide complementary information. Strong lensing is especially useful for measuring the mass concentrated near a cluster's center, while weak lensing can reveal how matter is distributed across its outer regions.
"Weak gravitational lensing can constrain mass much further out, so you can get a better picture of the surrounding cluster area," said Finner.
By combining these measurements with X-ray and radio observations from other telescopes, the scientists determined that XLSSC 122 is still undergoing a merger. Its galaxies are continuing to come together as the larger cluster takes shape.
The broader analysis also reinforced the earlier finding that an unusually large amount of mass is concentrated near the cluster's center.
Ancient Starlight Offers New Clues to Dark Matter
The team's third and most recent paper revealed another important feature of XLSSC 122: faint light produced by stars that are no longer bound to individual galaxies.
Known as intracluster light, this diffuse glow comes from stars scattered into the spaces between galaxies. Webb's observations represent the earliest known detection of intracluster light, providing another way to examine the development of galaxy clusters in the distant universe.
The widespread distribution of this light supports the conclusion that XLSSC 122 is undergoing a merger. As galaxies interact and collide, some stars are pulled away from their original galaxies and spread throughout the cluster. In XLSSC 122, many of these displaced stars appear not to have settled into its dense central region.
The researchers also uncovered an intriguing connection between these wandering stars and dark matter.
Near the cluster's center, the shape of the intracluster light closely matches the distribution of dark matter inferred from strong gravitational lensing. This suggests that the faint glow of stars between galaxies could potentially serve as a visible indicator of where invisible dark matter is con

articles.title_orig: Say Goodbye to Italy and Greece: This Unexpected Destination Is the World’s Fastest-Rising Travel Hotspot for 2027
articles.title_zh: Say Goodbye to Italy and Greece: This Unexpected Destination Is the World’s Fastest-Rising Travel Hotspot for 2027
articles.content_orig:
Forget the Amalfi Coast, Lisbon, or the Greek islands. According
to Skyscanner’s Travel Trends 2027 report, the world’s
fastest-rising destination is somewhere far less expected: Bishkek,
the capital of Kyrgyzstan.
Nestled at the foot of the Tian Shan mountains in Central Asia,
Bishkek has seen an astonishing 501% increase in flight searches,
putting it at the top of Skyscanner’s trending destinations for
2027.
With its leafy boulevards, spectacular mountain scenery,
fascinating history, and surprisingly affordable prices, this
under-the-radar capital might just be the next big thing in
travel.
Skyscanner analyzed millions of flight searches and surveyed
more than 28,000 travelers worldwide to identify the destinations
and experiences shaping travel in 2027.
The findings suggest that travelers are increasingly
prioritizing authentic experiences, outdoor adventures, and
destinations that offer better value for money.
Bishkek delivers on all three.
Often described as one of Central Asia’s greenest capitals, the
city combines Soviet-era architecture, bustling markets, trendy
cafés, and mountain views that seem almost too beautiful to be
real.
And unlike Europe’s increasingly crowded tourist hotspots,
Bishkek still feels relatively undiscovered.
One of Bishkek’s biggest attractions is its proximity to the
mountains.
Just outside the city, Ala-Archa National Park offers dramatic
alpine landscapes, glacier-fed rivers, and hiking trails surrounded
by towering peaks.
Whether you’re looking for a leisurely walk or a challenging
mountain trek, it’s an extraordinary escape from city life.
Travelers can also experience Kyrgyzstan’s nomadic traditions by
spending a night in a traditional yurt, horseback riding through
alpine meadows, or exploring the shores of Issyk-Kul, one of the
world’s largest high-altitude lakes.
For anyone dreaming of a digital detox, it’s difficult to
imagine a better setting.
Bishkek also serves as a gateway to Kyrgyzstan’s fascinating
Silk Road heritage.
Visitors can explore Ala-Too Square, wander through the city’s
leafy parks, and discover traditional crafts and local delicacies
at Osh Bazaar.
A short excursion brings travelers to Burana Tower, an
11th-century minaret that stands as a reminder of the region’s
medieval trading history.
Food is another highlight. Traditional dishes include lagman, a
hearty noodle dish, and plov, a flavorful rice dish often prepared
with meat and vegetables.
Best of all, dining out is remarkably affordable compared with
many popular European destinations.
Spring and early fall are particularly appealing, with
comfortable temperatures for sightseeing and outdoor
adventures.
Summer offers excellent conditions for trekking in the
mountains, while winter transforms the surrounding landscapes into
a snowy playground.
For American travelers, reaching Bishkek generally requires a
connecting flight, often through Istanbul or another international
hub. Travelers should check current entry requirements before
booking.

On the Newsquawk feed at 09:45 , 20 minutes before this page.
Official commentary of this kind is a staple of the post-agreement phase in EU-China trade relations: governments welcome the deal publicly while flagging that structural imbalances, the bilateral goods deficit being the standing German complaint, remain unresolved. The pattern in past episodes has been that such qualified endorsements carry little weight on their own; what has mattered for markets is whether the language precedes concrete follow-through such as tariff reviews, anti-subsidy actions, or procurement conditions, since that is where trade friction actually transmits into autos, capital goods, and the EUR-sensitive export complex. Germany's position is notable because its industrial exposure to China cuts both ways, which has historically made Berlin the softer voice in European trade debates relative to Brussels or Paris. The read-through for EUR is second order: bilateral deficit rhetoric of this sort has tended to move the single currency only when it escalates into measures with measurable volume effects. The tell is whether other member states or the Commission echo the deficit framing and whether any implementing instruments appear on the calendar.

articles.title_orig: Doctors warn against injury-prone China viral ‘flash step’ dance
articles.title_zh: Doctors warn against injury-prone China viral ‘flash step’ dance
articles.content_orig:
Veteran teacher says viral move appeals to the masses because it is both fun and witty – blending humour with professional skill
A dance move known as the “flash step” recently went viral on Chinese social media, inspiring countless imitations, memes and creative merchandise, including keychains.
In September, Chinese netizens jumped on the bandwagon, copying moves from a dance tutorial video made in the 1990s.
They were especially taken with three moves featured in the video: the “flash step”, “prodigal kicking the ball” and “black bear shaking fur”.
As its name vividly suggests, the flash step is a rapid, side-to-side dodging movement. “Prodigal kicking the ball” involves a rather bendy hopping kick with the arms outstretched, while “black bear shaking fur” features the dancer shaking vigorously, literally like a bear shaking its fur.

articles.title_orig: UnitedHealth Group tops estimates, hikes profit outlook as insurer manages high medical costs
articles.title_zh: UnitedHealth Group tops estimates, hikes profit outlook as insurer manages high medical costs
articles.content_orig:
UnitedHealth Group on Tuesday posted third-quarter earnings that blew past estimates and raised its full-year profit outlook, as the company continues to manage high medical costs and sees investments in value-based care and artificial intelligence take hold.
The nation's largest private insurer said it expects fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings of at least $20.50 per share, up from a previous outlook of $19.50 to $20 per share.
The healthcare giant's turnaround plan is gaining momentum after three consecutive strong quarters this year. UnitedHealth is working to stabilize margins by shrinking membership, exiting unprofitable contracts and ramping up investments in artificial intelligence and value-based care, which tie doctor and facility compensation to patient health outcomes, quality of care and cost effectiveness rather than the volume of medical services provided.
"You'll see in the quarter that we continue to execute not only on the financial aspects of our business, but really doing them with a simpler approach and an approach that's really focused on investing heavily in value-based care," CFO Wayne DeVeydt said in an interview.
Shares of the company rose about 3% in premarket trading.
Here's what the company reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
The company posted third-quarter net income of $4.11 billion, or $4.56 per share, compared with $2.35 billion, or $2.59 per share, in the same period a year ago. Excluding items like business divestitures, restructuring and the expected reduction of reserves for unprofitable contracts, UnitedHealth earned $4.69 per share.
Revenue fell to $112.69 billion from $113.16 billion in the prior-year quarter. The company's insurer, UnitedHealthcare, and its Optum healthcare unit both topped analysts' operating earnings estimates for the quarter, according to StreetAccount.
Notably, UnitedHealth's medical cost ratio — a measure of total medical expenses paid relative to premiums collected — came in at 88.4% for the third quarter. Analysts were expecting a ratio of 89.9% for the quarter, according to StreetAccount. A lower ratio typically indicates that the company collected more in premiums than it paid out in benefits, resulting in higher profitability.
Still, DeVeydt told CNBC that medical costs in the quarter "continue to be elevated versus historical norms" – an issue that has plagued insurers, particularly those operating privately run Medicare Advantage plans, for more than two years.
"I think it's something we should keep an eye on. I think you'll see that our medical care ratio has improved quite a bit, but I don't want that to be misleading in terms of [medical cost trends]," DeVeydt said.
He said the independent dispute resolution (IDR) process under the No Surprises Act is adding at least 100 basis points, or 1 percentage point, to total medical costs. That federal law, which took effect in 2022, aims to protect consumers from unexpected medical bills
The IDR process allows providers and insurers to resolve disputes over out-of-network payments. DeVeydt said those changes are driving up the company's claims costs, which can ultimately be passed on to consumers through higher premiums.
DeVeydt added that costs for inpatient services and pharmacy, particularly costly specialty pharmacy drugs for cancer and rare diseases, remain elevated.
Still, he highlighted the company's value-based care efforts, which are helping control medical costs by steering patients toward the right providers and emphasizing preventive care, DeVeydt added.
He said acute hospital admissions among UnitedHealth members fell 15% year over year through the third quarter, while home health admissions rose 10%, suggesting more patients are receiving care in lower-cost settings.
"You're finding more members are actually getting into a lower-cost care environment, but more importantly, they're getting into the care environment they actually want to be in," he told CNBC. "So we think we're really balancing both the quality and the cost."
UnitedHealth is also rolling out AI-powered ambient listening tools to reduce physicians' administrative burden and free up time for patient visits. Appointment scheduling done by patients rather than with the assistance of a provider increased 27% year over year, DeVeydt said.
He expects those initiatives to have a compounding effect on medical cost management through the fourth quarter and into 2027 as the programs expand.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Simon and Tropical Storm Rachel kill five people on Mexico’s Pacific coast
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Simon and Tropical Storm Rachel kill five people on Mexico’s Pacific coast
articles.content_orig:
Security forces use helicopters to rescue dozens of people as the two storms damage infrastructure and cause flash flooding
At least five people have died after Hurricane Simon and Tropical Storm Rachel pummelled Mexico’s Pacific coast, causing flooding that downed trees and electricity poles, blocked roads and inundated homes.
Simon claimed the life of a 71-year-old man who died when a wall collapsed in Chilpancingo in the southern state of Guerrero, governor Evelyn Salgado said at a press conference.
The storm also damaged infrastructure and homes in the state’s coastal towns, including the major seaport of Acapulco, she said.
Tropical Storm Rachel is blamed for the deaths of four members of one family, including two children, whose bodies were found on the outskirts of the city of Ensenada in Baja California, the state’s prosecutor’s office reported.
Five more people remained missing, while security forces used helicopters to rescue 32 people, prosecutors said. Baja governor Marina del Pilar said officials were helping more than 50 people in temporary shelters.
Simon did not make landfall and, after weakening to category two on the five-point Saffir-Simpson scale, was moving away from the coast, authorities said. A rain alert remained in place.
The National Hurricane Center in Miami said heavy rainfall associated with Simon in west-central Mexico over the next few days might still produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides.
Officials warned waves of up to five metres high were still expected in some coastal areas. Flooding and landslides had already hit communities close to rivers and streams in the states of Michoacan and Colima.
The El Niño phenomenon, characterised by rising water temperatures in the Pacific, is fuelling a more intense hurricanes this season in the region.
Meteorologists say the 2026-27 El Niño, which causes global changes in winds and rainfall as well as erratic weather conditions, is certain to be the biggest ever recorded. Scientists now also think human-caused global heating is making El Niños more intense.
With Agence France-Presse and Associated Press

articles.title_orig: World Athletics seeks two new members for Nominations Panel
articles.title_zh: World Athletics seeks two new members for Nominations Panel
articles.content_orig:
World Athletics is inviting applications for two independent members to join its Nominations Panel ahead of the next cycle of appointments to various World Athletics bodies.
Established in 2019 as part of World Athletics' governance reforms, the Nominations Panel is responsible for identifying, recruiting and assessing candidates for positions on World Athletics commissions, panels and other bodies, and making recommendations to the World Athletics Council.
The panel is being expanded to provide additional capacity and expertise, particularly in the lead-up to the 2027 World Athletics Election Congress. Following the expansion, it will comprise seven members, including five independent members.
World Athletics is seeking candidates with a strong background in athletics administration or significant experience in recruitment, appointments or human resources. Experience in sports administration is desirable.
The two successful candidates will be appointed by the World Athletics Council in December 2026, with their terms running until after the 2029 World Athletics Congress. The positions are voluntary and unpaid, with most of the panel's work conducted remotely.
Applications should include a CV, a covering letter outlining relevant experience, contact details and details of three referees.
Applications must be submitted to panel-candidates@worldathletics.org by 23:59 CET on Wednesday 4 November 2026.
Further information, including the full selection criteria and application requirements, can be found in the position description .

articles.title_orig: ‘She totally blew it’: How Kamala Harris wasted a year to make her case
articles.title_zh: ‘She totally blew it’: How Kamala Harris wasted a year to make her case
articles.content_orig:
Natasha previously reported on features, and UK news and politics. She became a full-time features writer in 2025, later joining the Washington bureau in 2026. She can be found on Instagram @natasha_leake
Kamala Harris’s husband has privately expressed a wish for her not to run for president again.
Doug Emhoff, 61, told people that he would prefer the former vice-president not to launch another White House bid, the Wall Street Journal reported. However, sources told the newspaper that he would support her if she decided to run.
Ms Harris has yet to declare whether she will seek the Democratic nomination in 2028, but has indicated that she is considering another campaign.
In July, she refused to rule out a presidential run when the Rev Al Sharpton asked her at the National Action Network conference in New York. “Listen, I might,” she replied.
She added: “I served for four years being a heartbeat away from the presidency of the United States. I know what the job is, and I know what it requires.”
A second campaign could prove divisive for the Democratic Party, with some within it believing it is time to put forward a fresh candidate after Ms Harris’s defeat by Donald Trump in 2024 .
In her memoir, 107 Days, which chronicles her abbreviated 2024 campaign, Ms Harris portrays her husband as a supportive and self-sacrificing partner.
When she was selected as Joe Biden’s running mate in 2020, Mr Emhoff gave up his job at a legal firm to avoid any suggestion of a conflict of interest.
“He made a huge sacrifice, gladly and without bitterness,” she wrote. “He knew it was essential that there be no appearance of conflicts of interest in our new roles. So that was his last day at his law firm.”
Mr Emhoff later returned to work as an attorney at Willkie Farr & Gallagher LLP in Los Angeles. The couple live in an $8m (£6m) home in Malibu overlooking the Pacific Ocean.
Gavin Newsom , the outgoing governor of California, is among those widely tipped as a contender for the Democratic nomination in 2028.
In September, Mr Newsom said he would not run if Ms Harris entered the race, describing the prospect of challenging her as a “waste of everyone’s time”.
“I wouldn’t run if she ran,” he told Jake Tapper of CNN.
“I wouldn’t do that to her. I wouldn’t do it to me. I wouldn’t do that to you. I wouldn’t waste everyone’s time,” he said.

articles.title_orig: In charts: How one of the world's biggest economies got trapped by debt
articles.title_zh: In charts: How one of the world's biggest economies got trapped by debt
articles.content_orig:
France's parliament begins debate on the 2027 budget Tuesday as high deficits, rising debt and student protests sharpen the political cost of fiscal consolidation.
The euro zone's second-biggest economy is barreling toward a debt crisis, and risks dragging the continent down with it, unless it sustainably brings down its national deficit, according to many market watchers.
Even as thousands take to the streets to protest years of underfunding in public services, particularly education, France has run one of Europe's highest deficit-to-GDP ratios for nearly a decade under President Emmanuel Macron.
Government spending remains well above its peers in the politically sensitive realm of social protections, particularly pensions and healthcare, while tepid economic growth has failed to compensate.
With presidential elections looming next year and parliamentarians proving reluctant to compromise, France's economic and political uncertainty is weighing on the euro .
French government borrowing costs have soared to their highest level in nearly a quarter of a century as jittery bond markets have responded to the country's failure to impose fiscal consolidation.
The widening gap in French bond yields over their German equivalents has raised questions over whether the European Central Bank would have to take the expensive and politically controversial step of intervening to stabilize the market. While this could halt a panic that fragments the currency union, the legacy of the Sovereign Debt Crisis — which hammered countries such as Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Italy — means it would require drastic action from France.
"The ECB will not step in just to 'bail out' France. If there was a European crisis they will intervene in some form but they will not save a country that cannot save itself," Antonio Fatas, professor of Economics at INSEAD Business School, said by email.
These charts show France's challenge.

articles.title_orig: IMF says AI boom driving world growth, but warns it's a ‘slow-moving tsunami' for jobs
articles.title_zh: IMF says AI boom driving world growth, but warns it's a ‘slow-moving tsunami' for jobs
articles.content_orig:
A motorcycle taxi rides past a banner at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center ahead of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group in Bangkok, Thailand, Friday, Oct. 9, 2026.
The International Monetary Fund on Tuesday slightly upgraded its outlook for the world economy for this year, while warning of growing risks from rising debt, including borrowing related to artificial intelligence.
The IMF says it expects the global economy to grow at a 3.1% pace this year. That's up from its July forecast for 3.0% growth and well below the 3.5% expansion in 2025. Growth in 2027 should rebound to 3.4%, it said in its latest Economic Outlook.
Stream NBC4 newscasts for free right here, right now.
The report, released as world economic and financial leaders gather in Bangkok for the fall meetings of the IMF and World Bank, predicts that growth in the United States will remain steady at 2.3% in 2026 and 2027.
Collectively, advanced economies will grow 2.1% this year, up from 2.0% in 2025. But growth is forecast to slow to 1.9% next year, it said.
The forecasts are based on a nearly 41% increase in oil prices this year, at an average of $96 a barrel. Global inflation is foreseen at 4.7% in 2026, falling to 4.1% next year. They also are based on the assumption that shipments of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz will resume by March, and that the boom in AI demand will moderate.
The boom in artificial intelligence is offsetting damage from sharply higher prices for oil and gas, IMF economists say, but it also carries risks.
The day's top national and international news.
Its benefits are not shared equally: the U.S. and China account for more than three-quarters of net demand for imports of computer chips and other AI-related equipment, the report said.
“The outlook is highly uneven,” Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF's director of research, told reporters in Bangkok.
Growth is increasingly concentrated, with 32 countries accounting for 95% of global growth, the report said. That compares with 54 countries as of April.
“The global economy is not simply slowing or accelerating; rather, growth is being reallocated across countries according to their exposure to the war-induced supply shock and AI-related demand strength,” it says.
Athanasios Vamvakidis, deputy director at the IMF's Monetary and Capital Markets Department, said an AI-related correction in stock markets is just one of the risks. Rising bond yields are another evolving problem, along with cyberthreats that could disrupt financial systems, he said.
Underscoring such concerns, sell-offs of AI-related shares swept through Asia on Tuesday, with South Korea's Kospi sinking as much as 7% before it closed 5.5% lower.
AI's effects on employment are another worry, “a slow moving tsunami, but a tsunami nonetheless,” IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said.
"The impact over time on jobs globally we estimate to be around 40% — jobs either augmented or downgraded or eliminated. And we are already seeing some of this impact,” she said.
Last week, the IMF chief urged countries both rich and poor to do a better job of improving their national finances, urging policymakers to do more to tame mounting levels of debt.
That's especially true at a time of high borrowing costs, Tenreyro said.
Countries that are somewhat insulated from the energy shocks of the Iran war and that are benefiting from rapid adoption of AI are managing to keep growth on track. But developing economies and emerging markets more vulnerable to higher costs for oil and gas will see growth slow to 3.7% this year from 4.5% in 2025, the report says. It forecasts they will regain momentum next year, expanding at a 4.4% annual pace.
The situation is much worse in the Middle East and Central Asia, where those regions' economies are expected to contract this year before recovering to a 6.3% rate of growth in 2027.
The 21 European countries that share the euro currency are expected to grow by 1.1% this year and 1.2% in 2027.
China, the world’s No. 2 economy, is expected to expand 4.5% this year, down from 5% in 2025, in line with the government's official target.
India is once again forecast to be the world’s fastest-growing major economy, advancing at a 7% clip, down from a sizzling 7.7% last year.
The IMF is a 191-nation lending organization that works to promote economic growth and financial stability and to reduce global poverty. At the meetings in Bangkok, finance ministers and central bank governors will assess the state of the world economy and discuss strategies to support financial stability and sustained growth.
AP journalists Haruka Nuga and Tian Macleod Ji contributed.

articles.title_orig: Gluon string breaking is simulated using trapped ions
articles.title_zh: Gluon string breaking is simulated using trapped ions
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for registering with Physics World If you'd like to change your details at any time, please visit My account
The particle-physics process of string breaking has been modelled on a trapped ion quantum computer by researchers in the US. The results are similar to previous findings obtained independently using neutral atom quantum simulators and superconducting quantum computers. The result suggests that traditional models of string breaking need to be modified slightly.
The strong interaction is the force that binds quarks together inside hadrons such as protons and neutrons. Unlike gravity, electromagnetism and the weak interaction, which all diminish with distance – its effect becomes stronger as particles are pulled apart. In quark–gluon plasma, where quarks and antiquarks swim in a sea of gluons, they are effectively free. However, when an isolated quark is pulled away from an isolated antiquark (or a proton, for example), the energy in the gluon field increases indefinitely. At some point, this energy grows large enough to create a new quark and antiquark. These bind to the original particles, leaving two hadrons. Free quarks are therefore never observed.
This process, in which the potential energy in the gluon field grows and grows until it is released with the creation of new matter, is known as string breaking. The theory of this mechanism was first outlined in 1951 by the future Nobel laureate Julian Schwinger . The process often underpins the formation of new particles in colliders, but its fundamental details remain poorly understood.
The notion of simulating experimentally inaccessible quantum processes using quantum processors has been discussed – and implemented for some systems – in the past few years. In 2025 scientists at Google Research in California and colleagues performed simplified calculations of the dynamics of string breaking using their Sycamore processor, which uses superconducting qubits, obtaining new insights into the process.
Also in 2025, researchers at the University of Innsbruck in Austria, together with colleagues at Harvard and the commercial company QuEra , took a slightly different tack. Instead of breaking the underlying quantum chromodynamic equations down into a series of discrete time steps and calculating their evolution, they used lasers to initialize the states of rubidium atoms such that their interaction would be analogous to quarks. This allowed them access to the dynamics of the string breaking process that would otherwise remain hidden.
Now, quantum-computing pioneer Christopher Monroe at Duke University in North Carolina and colleagues in the US and Belgium have achieved similar results to the QuEra group using trapped ions instead of neutral atoms. Monroe’s team modelled the behaviour of quarks using “domain walls” – regions where adjacent ions have opposite spins.
“You initialize the system with a certain number of domain walls, and then you apply the Hamiltonian – which means you do this QCD process – and you see how many domain walls you end up with. We show that the number actually increases.” Explains Arinjoy De , who was Monroe’s PhD student and now works at QuEra. To simulate the increasing energy in the gluon field as a quark is pulled away, the researchers used an external magnetic field: “We show that once you go beyond a certain threshold of the magnetic field, you go from two domain walls – or two particles – to create more particles,” says De.
The results suggest some modifications to the canonical theories of string breaking. Notably, they found that, contrary to the predictions of Schwinger, string breaking is initiated at the edges, where coupling to the quantum vacuum reduces the energetic cost of new particle creation, before propagating inwards to the bulk.
The researchers are now hoping that, with more qubits and greater circuit depth, they will be able to look at domain walls farther apart. This would allow them to study the inverse problem of string formation when particles collide: “Our theory colleagues Alexey Gorshkov and Zohreh Davoudi at the University of Maryland are really thinking a lot about these meson scattering experiments,” says Monroe.
Quantum computing researcher Boris Blinov of the University of Washington in Seattle says that the work is “significant in its own right as a demonstration of the potential of a quantum simulator in the future to do things faster than any classical analogue of it.” He says the current system is too small to outperform what can be achieved with a supercomputer but “with more qubits and this technology, this way of controlling qubits would be of significance at the very least for quantum chromodynamics, gauge theories and fundamental physics.”
Monroe and colleagues describe their work in Nature Physics .

articles.title_orig: Beyond Polarity: For a Marxist Theory of the World Order - Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research
articles.title_zh: Beyond Polarity: For a Marxist Theory of the World Order - Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research
articles.content_orig:
Collage by Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research drawing from a Dymaxion map projection and Islamic, Mesoamerican, Ethiopian, and Chinese maps made between the twelfth and seventeenth centuries.
Images sourced from: Muhammad al-Idrisi, Tabula Rogeriana, 1154, 1929 reconstruction and transliteration by Konrad Miller via Wikimedia Commons; Matteo Ricci and Li Zhizao, Kunyu Wanguo Quantu (坤輿萬國全圖), 1602, Library of Congress Geography and Map Division via Wikimedia Commons; Códice Xólotl, Lámina 1, Tetzcoco, Mexico, c. 1541 via Wikimedia Commons; Tigrayan circular map from the Māshafā Aksum (Book of Aksum), pre-eighteenth century, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Collection Antoine d’Abbadie, via Wikimedia Commons; and Justinkunimune, Blank World Map, Dymaxion Projection , 2023, Wikimedia Commons, CC0 1.0.
The maps in this dossier trace how the hegemonic world order has organised and represented the world, from colonialism, the post-World War II international order, and Cold War bipolarity to internationalised capital, the North–South divide, and US unipolarity. More than representations, they distil concepts imperial and colonial powers have used to exercise power. Every dot of ink is a choice: what sits at the centre, which countries appear at the top, and which distortions are considered acceptable. The cover gathers cartographic traditions with different centres, orientations, and cosmologies, asking how, beyond poles and blocs, we might understand the unequal social relations that constitute the world order itself.
The Mercator projection was developed in 1569 for European navigation during the colonial period. During imperial expansion, it became the standard map projection, still used today. This map, which shows the spheres of influence of the ‘great powers’ and their ‘possessions’, was created by H.E.C. Robinson in 1908. Sourced from the National Library of Australia via Wikimedia Commons.
The language of ‘unipolarity’ and ‘multipolarity’ – whether global power is concentrated in one dominant state or distributed among several major states – has become almost unavoidable in political debates. US and allied policymakers have often described the post-Cold War international system as a ‘liberal international order’ increasingly threatened by ‘revisionist powers’ such as China and Russia. Many governments and movements in the Global South, by contrast, welcome what they see as the emergence of a multipolar world in which Washington can no longer dictate the terms of international life. This aspiration is understandable. Any weakening of the United States’ capacity to impose blockades and unilateral sanctions, organise coups, and wage wars can open political space for sovereign development and for class struggles to advance.
‘Multipolarity’ may function as a slogan of resistance to US primacy and offer a rough description of how certain forms of state power are distributed. Its political appeal, however, should not be confused with explanatory power. The number of powerful states tells us little about the social relations that produce their power, the class interests organised within them, or the imperialist hierarchies that connect them. Multipolarity does not, by itself, provide a Marxist account of the world; when treated as such, it can mislead us into believing that a wider distribution of state power is inherently progressive. 1
Venezuela’s former President Hugo Chávez, who had every reason to welcome a world of many centres, was dissatisfied enough with the term ‘multipolarity’ to coin ‘pluripolarity’ against it – insisting that what mattered was not the number of centres but whether popular subjects were the agents of transformation. 2 The need to specify this political content was itself revealing: the number of poles alone tells us nothing about the class forces or popular subjects shaping the resulting order.
A Marxist analysis must therefore replace the arithmetic of poles with the analysis of a chain: an unevenly developed system of social formations, each internally constituted by class struggle and externally bound to the others by relations of exploitation and dependence. The question is not how many poles there are but how the chain is held together and where it is most susceptible to being broken.
The problem, then, lies in the image of the pole itself. It asks us to picture the international system as a set of sovereign states treated as its decisive units, each possessing a measurable quantity of power. Depending on how that power is distributed, the system is described as unipolar, bipolar, or multipolar. This vocabulary tells us how many great powers count as geopolitical poles. It does not tell us what kind of social order each state reproduces, how its power is produced, which class interests shape that power, or through which transnational relations it is exercised. It photographs the chessboard while hiding the social relations that made the board, carved the pieces, and decided who is permitted to play.
Polarity presents itself as a form of measurement. Measured by gross domestic product (GDP) at purchasing power parity (PPP) – which adjusts for differences in price levels between countries – the world appears economically plural: no single economy commands anything resembling the dominance that the word ‘unipolarity’ implies. Measured by military expenditure and the alliance systems organised around it, however, that same world appears far more concentrated: in 2022, the United States alone accounted for about 53.5% of global military spending, while the US-led military bloc accounted for 74.3%. The United States also maintained at least 902 foreign military bases – by far the world’s largest network. 3
Measured in a third way – by control over critical markets and infrastructures that function as chokepoints in contemporary production and exchange – the world appears neither plural nor bipolar but close to monopolistic. Yet this concentration does not map neatly onto states. Four firms hold 56% of the world’s commercial seed market and 61% of the global pesticide market. One of them is Bayer, which absorbed Monsanto and its patent portfolio in 2018. 4 Three firms – Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, and Sanofi – control more than 90% of the global insulin market by value and around 95% of the market in low- and middle-income countries. 5 Palantir, a single US firm, supplies the data platform on which the US Army runs its operations and US immigration authorities track human beings. 6
The same concentration appears in finance and energy. The dollar accounts for more than four-fifths of global trade finance – a predominance that far exceeds the US share of global output or trade. This is a form of monetary command that a ranking of national economic weight cannot capture. 7 In energy, ownership of a resource can likewise diverge from control over the circuits through which it reaches the market. This divergence is visible in neighbouring Venezuela and Guyana. Venezuela has owned its oil outright since 1976, yet US aggression – whether military (such as the 3 January bombing), economic (over 1,000 sanctions and other unilateral coercive measures), or otherwise – continues to shape the conditions under which Venezuelan oil can be sold internationally. In neighbouring Guyana, the 2016 production-sharing agreement governing the offshore Stabroek Block restricts the government’s ability to alter its terms without the prior written consent of the ExxonMobil-led consortium. 8
Three measurements, three different worlds, one reality. The disagreement between those who see unipolarity and those who see multipolarity is therefore not simply a disagreement about the facts. It is also a disagreement about which relations constitute power – and it is precisely this question, which must be settled before any counting can begin, that the vocabulary of poles leaves unanswered.
Polarity also inherits what is often called a Westphalian repres

On October 1 (local time), the all-new TUCSON World Premiere took place in New York with the Manhattan skyline as its backdrop. With global media and influencers in attendance, TUCSON took to the runway with a striking presence fit for ‘The Boldest SUV.’
The World Premiere aimed to consistently deliver TUCSON’s ‘The Boldest’ message, highlighting its capability to accommodate both complex urban scenarios and outdoor lifestyles. Within the U.S., TUCSON’s largest market for sales, New York became the stage as a city where opportunities are given to those bold enough to take on a challenge. From the journey toward the venue to the unveiling, exhibition, and hands-on experiences of the vehicles, every chapter offered a vivid look at TUCSON’s bold character.
Media and influencers stepped aboard a ferry for a special journey across the East River, overlooking the Manhattan skyline. Arriving at the dock, oversized typography decorating the venue’s exterior wall caught eyes and set the scene for a grand entrance. As the main event began, TUCSON’s standard model and the off-road-inspired XRT PRO took to the runway, drawing the audience deeper into the experience.
In his opening speech, José Muñoz, President and CEO of Hyundai Motor Company, outlined a vision for future growth built on the strong business performance of Hyundai Motor Group and Hyundai Motor Company. Highlighted were major investment plans spanning the U.S. and Korea, together with the expansion of future businesses centered on robotics. He then unveiled TUCSON, a global bestselling model that will make that vision possible.
SangYup Lee, Head of Hyundai and Genesis Global Design, offered an in-depth look at the inspiration behind TUCSON and the craft that brought it to life. Its bold exterior shaped by the ‘Art of Steel’ design language, its intuitive and safety-focused cabin guided by the ‘Art of Comfort’, and the rugged character of the XRT PRO together define a new direction for an SUV capable both in the city and in the great outdoors.
JinHwan Jung, Head of Vehicle Development Tech Unit 2, underscored the development goal of delivering uncompromised value, led by the Next-generation Hybrid System’s fuel efficiency and driving performance—‘Intelligent Efficiency.’
Eric Wood, Head of Product Experience at 42dot, then shared the vision for Pleos Connect ‘Everyday Progress,’ designed to elevate daily life through continuous updates.
Also displayed outdoors on the pier, TUCSON stood in harmony with the Manhattan nightscape, its boldness coming into sharp focus. Indoors, early sketches revealed the thinking behind the design, while a full-scale transmission model showcased the core of the Next-generation Hybrid System.
Guests also stepped into the vehicles to explore the key functions of Pleos Connect firsthand. Across the outdoor and indoor spaces, media and influencers examined the vehicles and exhibits in depth, capturing the details that define TUCSON.
The World Premiere delivered an impactful introduction to the all-new TUCSON as Hyundai Motor Company’s hero model, spotlighting its bold design, hybrid technology and Pleos Connect that set it apart from the competition. Now, a new journey begins for ‘The Boldest SUV’—one that will bring greater value to everyday life for customers around the world.

articles.title_orig: Bill Gates: Technology is a world in need of governance
articles.title_zh: Bill Gates: Technology is a world in need of governance
articles.content_orig:
âWe are not paying enough attention to the risksâ of artificial intelligence âand weâre not doing enough to minimize the harms. We are also not doing enough to take advantage of the current opportunities with AI,â says Bill Gates, cofounder and former CEO of Microsoft, in an interview Vatican News.
The tech leader also spoke about Pope Leo XIVâs encyclical Magnifica humanitas , saying âWhat struck me is that the Pope isnât saying âstop AIâ. Heâs making a more careful argument: that we need to actively preserve whatâs human in the face of it. That lines up with something Iâve been arguing myselfâ.
Read the full interview (lightly edited for length and clarity):
Q: Mr Gates, in recent weeks, many voices from within the technology industry have raised concerns about the potential dangers associated with the further development of artificial intelligence. What is your view?
Bill Gates: It is striking how people inside the industry are voicing their concerns. These are people who are competing with each other and disagree on many issues, but here, theyâre saying the same thing: This is not something the industry can self-regulate, it must be led by neutral actors, primarily governments. The trouble is most people in government donât fully understand how the technology works.
Itâs my view that we are not paying enough attention to the risks, and weâre not doing enough to minimize the harms. We are also not doing enough to take advantage of the current opportunities with AI. The [Bill and Melinda Gates] Foundation released our annual Goalkeepers Report last month, and it made the case that AI could be a great equalizer or widen existing gaps between rich and poor.
AI can do things like let rural doctors use a smartphone as an ultrasound machine, provide personalized tutoring that adapts to how a student actually learns, and offer advice tailored to a farmerâs own soil and weather. But none of that happens automatically.
Left to the market, the most capable tools will get built first for whoever can pay the most, not for whoever needs them most. Thatâs why we committed a billion dollars over the next two years to push AI toward health, education, and agriculture in the places market forces would reach last. The risk and the opportunity are moving at the same speed, and we have to act on both at once.
Q: More generally, how do you see the future of an increasingly technology-driven society?
AI is different from any other technology weâve seen before. With past innovations like the PC or the internet, the pattern has started with some major disruption, but eventually it works out, and people end up with better tools. AI is different. Itâs more like an evolutionary event. Weâve created a kind of intelligence that in many ways matches or exceeds human cognition. Treating it as just âthe next PCâ causes people to underestimate it entirely.
We can think about it as two different periods. Right now, weâre in a transition where we donât yet have the upside at a large scale everywhere, but we do have real disruption. Thatâs truer in rich countries than in lower-income ones.
In the places where the Foundation conducts our work, the benefits can arrive faster than the disruption does, because there was so much unmet need to begin with. That only works, though, if we fix things like how most AI models were trained overwhelmingly on English and badly underserve the billions of people who speak other languages.
So real change is required during this period, on multiple fronts, including how we tax labour versus automation, which jobs we deliberately reserve for humans, and how we make sure the technology actually reaches the people whoâd benefit most, not just the people who can pay the most.
Then, on the other side of that transition, if we get the guardrails and the access right, we could see a world of genuine abundance: AI and humanoid robots handling food, shelter, and other basics.
That period will raise a totally different set of questions about meaning and how people spend their time. My focus right now is getting us through the next several years without a catastrophic bioterrorism attack or cyber-security event, and without leaving huge parts of the job market, or huge parts of the world, behind.
Q: President Trump, by contrast, has minimized the potential risks of further AI development. Do you agree with his position? What role should political leaders play in this debate?
This is technology thatâs more dangerous than nuclear weapons, and has the potential to be more beneficial than nuclear energy. Adding basic safety checks costs us almost no speed, and it cuts the risk a lot. Thatâs a trade worth making.
Government leaders need to first agree on the basic facts, that there are real dangers here, and real benefits, and then discuss details of the response. We need more AI expertise inside governments, governments working with industry, and governments working together, because no country wants bioterrorism or a cyberattack that takes down its own infrastructure.
I worry that it may take a serious cyberattack or a bad bioterrorism incident before the political system takes this as seriously as it needs to.
Q: Is there any connection between the risks associated with the development of AI and your decision to step away from any operational role at Microsoft?
No, my decision was a gradual, planned shift toward philanthropy and my work at the Gates Foundation, which happened more than a decade ago.
Q: Have you read Pope Leoâs encyclical Magnifica humanitas ? Do you agree with its reflections on artificial intelligence?
Yes, I read it, and I wrote about it in my own memo in August. I was fascinated by it. It lays a strong foundation for the work that needs to be done. What struck me is that the Pope isnât saying âstop AI.â Heâs making a more careful argument: that we need to actively preserve whatâs human in the face of it. That lines up with something Iâve been arguing myself.
There are certain roles, like caretaking of children, serving as a judge or a juror, and some parts of medicine, where the relationship itself is the point. We shouldnât hand those over just because a model becomes capable enough to do them.
I am very glad to see the Catholic Church, and other religious groups, so engaged in the AI debate; I believe their engagement is critical to ensuring that AI serves everyone in the most equitable way.
