articles.title_orig: Robert E. Hall wins Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
articles.title_zh: Robert E. Hall wins Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
articles.content_orig:
Berkeley’s world-class economics department is celebrating the Nobels won today by two scholars: Robert E. Hall, a 1964 graduate and early-career faculty member, and Michael Woodford, a visiting scholar in the 2025-26 academic year.
When the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences today announced the two winners of Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, the UC Berkeley economics community celebrated them as scholars who have achieved the heights of economic influence — and as colleagues with deep connections to the campus.
Robert E. Hall was an accomplished young scholar who earned his bachelor’s degree at UC Berkeley in 1964, and served on the economics faculty from 1967-1970 before moving to MIT and then to Stanford University. Michael Woodford, a scholar at Columbia University, was a deeply important teacher and mentor for some of Berkeley top young faculty economists even before coming to Berkeley as a visiting scholar last year.
Their remarkable careers, capped with the Nobel announcement yesterday, underscore the historic, extended influence of the Berkeley economics department in the 1960s — and affirm that Berkeley today is a robust center of contemporary economics, attracting some of the world’s most important scholars.
Six Berkeley economists have previously won the Nobel: David Card (2021), Oliver Williamson, (2009), George Akerlof (2001), Daniel McFadden (2000), John C. Harsanyi (1994) and Gérard Debreu (1983). Notably, James A. Robinson of the University of Chicago won the prize in 2024, honored in part for work on development economics that he had done from 1999-2004 while on the Berkeley faculty.
The Swedish Academy this year honored Hall and Woodford for what their scholarship tells policymakers about stabilizing the economy in turbulent times.
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” said John Hassler, chair of the academy’s Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences. “With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume.”
Hall, now 83, was born in Palo Alto. His selection crystallizes how profoundly important the 1960s were for Berkeley economics — and how the influence of that era resonates even today.
It was an extraordinary time, a gathering of titans. Debreau and Harsanyi were senior professors. Dale Jorgenson was on the faculty in that era; he’d won the John Bates Clark Medal, seen as the second highest honor for an economist, and was seen as a Nobel contender.
Williamson, McFadden and Peter Diamond were all young assistant professors, and Diamond would later win a Nobel while at MIT. Hall’s fellow student and Class of ’64 graduate, Thomas J. Sargent , would win the Nobel in 2011 for research on cause and effect in macroeconomics.
Even as an undergrad, Hall was making innovative contributions. He began research with Jorgenson that would lead to the seminal 1967 paper, “Tax Policy and Investment Behavior.”
The paper was “an instant classic,” said Michael Reich, who joined the Berkeley economics faculty in the fall of 1974 and now serves as Chair of the Center on Wage and Employment Dynamics. “It was required reading when I took a public finance class at Harvard in 1968, and it is still cited as a major contribution.”
Even after landing at Stanford, Hall maintained connections at Berkeley. For example, he delivered a talk at the centennial celebration of the economics department in 2002 and gave the department’s commencement address in 2006, when it was chaired by Ben Hermalin, now Berkeley’s executive vice chancellor and provost .
Woodford’s connection to Berkeley is more recent. Now 71, he arrived at Columbia by way of the University of Chicago, Yale Law School and MIT, where he earned his Ph.D.  For the 2025-26 academic year, Woodford was a visiting scholar at UC Berkeley.
“He is intellectually close to all of our macro group and also to the behavioral group,” said Stefano DellaVigna, the current chair of economics. “One way to think of his recent work in this area is that he builds on evidence from cognitive science and neuroscience on how people actually process information, and is able to show that getting that right really matters for understanding how people would process macroeconomic information, such as on inflation or economic growth.”
Woodford also spent time on the faculty at Princeton — that’s where he served as undergraduate thesis advisor to Emi Nakamura and Jón Steinsson in 2000 and 2001. Both are now on the Berkeley faculty.
Nakamura credits Woodford with encouraging her to focus on macroeconomics; she won the Clark Medal in 2019.
“The questions he asked about monetary policy were so interesting that it changed how I thought about economics as a whole,” Nakamura recounted. “As a thesis advisor, he was incredibly generous. I remember when I was working on my undergraduate thesis, struggling to understand the logic of one of the standard equations in the model, I sent him an email on December 24th, not expecting to hear back, of course. But he did write back — and really helped me understand what these equations were meant to represent.
“Later on in my career, I became increasingly aware of the impact that his work on monetary policy had on practical monetary policymaking around the world. My guess is that his research has had more practical impact on policymaking than almost any other economist. Anyone who visits a central bank almost anywhere in the world today is aware of this.”
After her studies, Nakamura joined the Columbia faculty, where Woodford became an important colleague.
“I remember a number of conversations I had with him at critical points in my own research, where he gave me some insight or encouragement that made a big difference,” she said. “Sometimes it was just a short conversation, but sometimes it was an insight that made all the difference. He was an amazing colleague to have.”

articles.title_orig: Mamdani orders review of NYPD's use-of-force policies as progressives call for greater change
articles.title_zh: Mamdani orders review of NYPD's use-of-force policies as progressives call for greater change
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK CITY (WABC) -- Mayor Zohran Mamdani has directed the NYPD to conduct its first comprehensive review of use-of-force policies and practices in a decade and announced a series of reforms aimed at strengthening accountability for officers accused of serious misconduct.
The review, which will take place over the coming months, comes as the administration faces mounting pressure from some supporters to follow through on campaign promises related to policing, including calls to dismantle the NYPD's Strategic Response Group. The mayor also said he has no plans to remove Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch.
According to the mayor's office, the review will include a community engagement process and examine how the department's use-of-force policies are applied and whether changes are needed. The administration said it is the first such review in 10 years.
The changes come after scrutiny of an NYPD officer's retirement following the fatal police shooting of Win Rozario , a 19-year-old who was suffering an apparent psychiatric episode when officers were called to his Ozone Park, Queens, home in May 2024. Rozario was shot and killed after he lunged at officers with a pair of scissors.
The officers were cleared by the state attorney general, but the Civilian Complaint Review Board later concluded that they used excessive force.
One of the officers, Salvatore Alongi, was allowed to retire before he could face an administrative trial because the NYPD failed to inform the review board. NYPD Commissioner Tisch acknowledged the failure as an oversight.
Mamdani said the reforms are intended to increase accountability within the department.
"When the government uses force against a New Yorker, the standard for accountability must be at its highest," he said. "Every New Yorker deserves to know that force will be used lawfully, carefully and only when necessary."
In addition to reviewing use-of-force guidelines, the department will strengthen pending retirement notifications. The city will increase funding for the inspector general that monitors the NYPD, and the department will standardize public disclosure protocols for police-involved incidents.
Ninety percent of New York City police officers go their entire careers without a single substantiated civilian complaint. The police union said that number would be even higher if the Civilian Complaint Review Board took what it called an "unbiased" approach.
"There should be no review of the NYPD's use of force policies," said the PBA president, "without a corresponding review of the blatantly biased and unjust way those policies are interpreted by the Civilian Complaint Review Board."
Critics, however, said the mayor's reforms do not go far enough.
Loyda Colon, executive director of the Justice Committee, a support network for victims of police violence, said a broader overhaul is needed.
"Does there need to be a full overhaul of the NYPD discipline process? Yes, but that's also after the fact. There's good intent here, but this is far from enough."

articles.title_orig: Alternative gravity theory offers possible explanation for dark energy changing over time
articles.title_zh: Alternative gravity theory offers possible explanation for dark energy changing over time
articles.content_orig:
BBC Science turned to a physicist at the University of Cincinnati for context about dark energy, which scientists say makes up 70% of the universe.
UC College of Arts and Sciences Assistant Professor Jessica Muir was among a group of 400 scientists from around the world who took part in the Dark Energy Survey led by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory.
They used powerful high-altitude telescopes to survey the night sky between 2013 and 2019, cataloguing hundreds of millions of galaxies to calculate the distribution of matter in the universe. By studying patterns of structure in the universe, researchers hope to provide some answers about dark energy.
Not all physicists agree with the prevailing theories surrounding dark energy.
The BBC spoke to physicist David Wiltshire at the University of Canterbury, who argues that the universe isn't consistently homogeneous in every corner. He argues the clumping of galaxies might explain why the universe appears to be expanding at a faster rate since time is relative to gravity.
UC Assistant Professor Jessica Muir. Photo/Provided
Muir is working hard to find ways to explain the seeming paradoxes surrounding dark energy. Muir has a background in applied mathematics, earning a master’s degree from Cambridge University before she earned a doctoral degree in physics. Muir contributed to the data analysis for the Dark Energy Survey using UC’s Advanced Research Computing Center.
“There are things in our model that don’t make sense,” Muir told the BBC . “It’s not very satisfying that we don’t know what 95 per cent of the Universe is made of.”
But she told the BBC she isn't ready to dismiss dark energy and Albert Einstein's prevailing notions on the cosmological constant yet.
“It would be very exciting if we say, ‘Oh, we missed this thing, and it turns out we don’t need a mysterious substance that has negative pressure and that makes up 70 per cent of the mass and energy in the universe,'” Muir told the BBC.
Muir elaborated on her BBC interview this week.
“More excitingly, in my opinion, is that new cosmology results in the last couple years have shown a preference for time-evolving dark energy properties,“ she said.
“This would require an extension of our model of dark energy beyond the simplest 'cosmological standard model,' in which dark energy is described as a cosmological constant,“ Muir said.
“If this is the case, it would be a huge deal, but it certainly isn't a rejection of the prevailing theory of dark energy,“ she said. “It's a step towards building a more fundamental understanding of the physics of this mysterious substance that makes up 70% of the energy density in our Universe — and understanding what the available data can tell us about it.“

articles.title_orig: Duo Share Nobel in Economics for Work on Steering Through Booms and Busts
articles.title_zh: Duo Share Nobel in Economics for Work on Steering Through Booms and Busts
articles.content_orig:
English English (pdf) Swedish Swedish (pdf)
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has decided to award the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2026 to
Robert E. Hall Stanford University, CA, USA.
Michael Woodford Columbia University, New York, USA.
“for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”
This year’s laureates in the economic sciences, Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford, have developed new macroeconomic models that have significantly improved our ability to implement effective stabilisation policy. On the basis of these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the economy’s peaks and troughs.
The economy is characterised by alternating downturns and upturns. Ever since the economist John Maynard Keynes launched his theories almost a century ago, stabilisation policy has been important for tackling these fluctuations. During recessions, the economy is boosted by reducing interest rates and increasing the budget deficit, while the opposite should be done to slow a booming economy.
However, during the oil crises of the 1970s, it seemed that the Keynesian models that govern when and how measures should be implemented no longer worked. They did not reduce unemployment, but led to uncontrolled inflation instead. The West experienced a decade of low growth, high unemployment and high inflation. Many people believed that stabilisation policy had done more harm than good and that it should be retired.
Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford are awarded this year’s prize in economic sciences for demonstrating how economic models could be reconstructed to revitalise stabilisation policy. Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation. This encompasses an understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions.
A central component in these models is that households and businesses are forward looking when making decisions about savings or product prices. When governments and central banks communicate their plans for economic policy, they can influence this view of the future and move the economy in the right direction. Since the new models’ introduction, they have been extremely helpful in dealing with the economic downturns that have affected us.
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” says John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.

articles.title_orig: You Can Now Set Up Your iPhone Duo Pre-Order - Do It Before Friday
articles.title_zh: You Can Now Set Up Your iPhone Duo Pre-Order - Do It Before Friday
articles.content_orig:
Apple has opened its "Get Ready" service for iPhone Duo pre-orders, allowing customers to pre-select a variety of options to streamline the process of ordering and have a better chance of grabbing one on launch day.
The iPhone Duo launches on October 23, while pre-orders go live on October 16 at 5 a.m. Pacific Time or 8 a.m. Eastern Time. Rather than turn up on the day, however, Apple encourages customers to take action before then and increase the chances of securing their preferred model on day one of sales.
Get Ready is an option available on Apple's online store and in its Apple Store app , and it lets you select a preferred color and capacity ahead of time. It also lets you confirm your carrier status, choose your accessories, pick an AppleCare+ plan, select a trade-in, add a payment method, and set a shipping and billing address.
Get Ready is really helpful because when pre-orders go live, it allows you to essentially perform a one-tap order. That's a real advantage when it comes to iPhone Duo, given that supplies are expected to be limited.
It's been said before about other iPhones, but pre-orders of the iPhone Duo really could sell out within minutes – there have been multiple reports of production issues leading to supply constraints, and users who have completed Get Ready will be able to submit orders faster.
So if you're set on being one of the first to get hold of Apple's debut foldable, make sure to visit Apple's website or Apple Store app and complete the Get Ready process now.
